title: GBP2 condensates promote ferroptosis to sensitize anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy in melanoma

paper_content.abstract: The mechanisms underlying the limited response to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) remain unclear. One explanation is that tumors escape cytotoxic T cell killing by disrupting interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) signaling. Here we show that guanylate-binding protein 2 (GBP2), an IFN-γ–inducible molecule, functions as a general amplifier of T cell–mediated cytotoxicity by promoting ferroptosis in melanoma. GBP2 enhances STAT1 activation and suppresses SLC7A11, thereby sensitizing tumor cells to ferroptotic death. Upon IFN-γ stimulation, GBP2 undergoes phase separation through an intrinsically disordered region, forming condensates that sequester SHP1 and sustain STAT1 activation. Disrupting GBP2 phase separation impairs ferroptosis, accelerates tumor growth, and weakens T cell–driven tumor control. GBP2 also increases HMGB1 release from ferroptotic cells, promoting cytotoxic T cell infiltration. These findings identify GBP2 as a key mediator linking IFN-γ signaling to ferroptosis and demonstrate that enhancing this pathway can improve tumor responsiveness to ICB immunotherapy.
paper_content.introduction:
Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), exemplified by inhibitors targeting programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) or programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1), has emerged as a transformative therapeutic approach1. ICB therapy restores or enhances the function of effector CD8+T cells (cytotoxic T lymphocytes, CTL) and drives interferon-γ (IFN-γ) production to eliminate tumor cells. Despite substantial clinical success, a significant subset of melanoma patients exhibit suboptimal responses. The pre-existing immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) remains a major barrier to efficacy, driven by factors such as low expression of immune checkpoints and neoantigens, genomic instability, tumor mutational burden, limited infiltration of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs), and attenuated IFN-γ gene signature2,3. These challenges underscore the urgent need for combinatorial strategies capable of overcoming TME‑associated resistance and broadening the benefit of ICB.

One promising approach to elicit this transformation is to induce ferroptosis in tumor cells. Ferroptosis is an iron‑dependent form of cell death driven by lethal accumulation of lipid peroxides4. Multiple strategies have been employed to trigger ferroptosis, including inhibition or degradation of ferroptosis suppressor glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), development of novel sensitizers for ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1), blockade of system X −, and therapeutic cancer nanovaccines—all of which have shown synergistic effects with ICB therapy in preclinical cancer models5. Recently, Wang et al. demonstrated that type II IFN signaling serves as an effective entry point to amplify ferroptosis6. However, the precise molecular mechanisms by which IFN-γ enhances ferroptosis remain poorly understood.

Emerging evidence suggests that many molecular assemblies form membraneless biomolecular condensates via phase separation, offering an insight into previously unexplained biological phenomena7–9. Dysregulated phase separation has been increasingly recognized as a key contributor to cancer progression, including modulation of immune responses8,10,11. Moreover, recent studies indicate that phase separation can facilitate ferroptosis, raising the possibility that this process may serve as a regulatory hub12,13. Nonetheless, the mechanisms by which phase separation selectively compartmentalizes signaling components to control ferroptotic activity remain largely elusive.

In this study, to identify candidate targets for combinatorial immunotherapy, we applied weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA) to screen hub genes associated with IFN-γ response and CTL cytolytic activity. Guanylate binding protein 2 (GBP2) was emerged as a key gene of interest. We observed that GBP2 expression positively correlated with CTL cytotoxicity and infiltration. GBP2 overexpression enhanced, whereas GBP2 deletion attenuated, ferroptosis induced by ICB‑activated CTLs. Mechanistically, we reveal an IFN‑γ–dependent pathway in which tumor cell GBP2 undergoes phase separation, sequestering SHP1 to promote STAT1 phosphorylation. This signaling cascade drives immunogenic ferroptosis, thereby potentiating the efficacy of anti–PD‑L1 immunotherapy. Our findings establish GBP2 phase separation as a previously unrecognized molecular circuit that mediates IFN-γ-dependent ferroptosis and highlight GBP2 as a promising target for combinatorial melanoma immunotherapy.
paper_content.results:
WGCNA identified GBP2 as a CTL cytolytic activity associated gene in melanoma

ICB therapy primarily eliminates tumor cells by enhancing the effector function of CTL. Activated CTLs engage multiple cytolytic pathways, including IFN-γ, perforin-granzyme, and Fas-Fas ligand signaling to eradicate tumor cells14. However, tumors frequently evade this immune pressure by impairing CTL cytolytic activity—either through inducing T cell dysfunction in CTL-high tumors or by preventing T cell infiltration in CTL-low tumors6. To identify molecular targets associated with CTL cytolytic activity, we employed WGCNA, a robust strategy for screening candidate genes linked to phenotypic traits15. Fifteen co‑expression modules were identified (Figs. 1A and S1). Among them, the yellow module exhibited the strongest correlation with 6-gene-IFN-γ signature (R=0.89, P=4e-29), cytolytic activity signature (R=0.81, P=7e-21) and two independent cytotoxic cell signatures (R=0.86, P=9e-26 and R=0.81, P=3e-20), as determined by module eigengene analysis (Fig. 1B and Supplementary Dataset 1). These signatures collectively predict CTL cytolytic activity16–19. Gene Ontology biological process (GO-BP) analysis further revealed that yellow module genes were significantly enriched in immune regulation, cell killing and IFN-γ response (Fig. 1C). These findings indicate that the yellow module represents a central network associated with CTL cytotoxicity, warranting further interrogation of its constituent genes for hub gene identification.

GO molecular function (MF) analysis showed additional enrichment of GTP binding and GTPase activity in the yellow module (Fig. 1C). GTP-binding proteins regulate a wide range of cellular processes, and elevated GTP levels have recently been linked to be associated with tumor progression, chemotherapy resistance, and ICB resistance20–22. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of the PRJEB23709 cohort demonstrated that GTPase activity and GTP binding were significantly positive enriched in ICB responders (Fig. 1D). Based on this, all yellow module genes were intersected with known GTP-binding proteins, yielding 18 candidates (Fig. 1E). Univariate Cox analysis identified guanylate binding protein 2 (GBP2) as the gene most significantly associated with overall survival (OS) in melanoma patients (Fig. 1F). This finding was validated in GSE8401, GSE59455, and GSE54467 cohorts, with consistent results (Fig. S2A–C). In the GSE65904 cohort, patients with low GBP2 expression exhibited shorter distant metastasis free survival (DMFS) and disease-specific survival (DSS) compared to those with high GBP2 expression (Fig. S2D).

We next examined the relationship between GBP2 expression and clinical features. In the GSE3189 dataset, GBP2 expression was significantly higher in normal tissues than in melanoma tissues (Fig. S2E). Spatial transcriptomic analysis of a melanoma specimen, segmented into malignant, boundary and non-malignant regions and annotated with 10 cell types, revealed that GBP2 was predominantly expressed in normal epithelial cells, with markedly lower levels in malignant regions (Fig. 1G–I). Analysis of major pathological prognostic factors demonstrated that higher GBP2 expression was associated with favorable clinical features, including reduced Breslow thickness, lower Clark level and ulceration—all indicators of better prognosis (Fig. S2F)23,24. To explore the potential biological functions of GBP2 in melanoma, we conducted GSEA and GO analyses. Across six independent cohorts, patients with high GBP2 expression showed significant enrichment in IFN-γ response, regulation of immunity and cell killing (Figs. S3 and S4). Together, these bioinformatic findings in clinical samples identify GBP2 as a potential prognostic biomarker and reveal its close association with CTL cytolytic activity in melanoma.

GBP2 deletion inhibited the CTL-induced ferroptosis to blunt the efficacy of ICB

We next investigated the relationship between GBP2 and ICB responsiveness in melanoma. GBP2 knockout (GBP2−/−) lines were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 in B16-ovalbumin (OVA). GBP2 overexpressing (GBP2oe) lines were established via lentiviral transduction in both B16-ovalbumin (OVA) and A375 cells (Fig. S5A, B and Supplementary Table 1). To investigate the role of GBP2 in antitumor immunity, we first assessed its function in immunodeficient NOD. Cg-Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice. GBP2 knockout exhibited growth kinetics comparable to control tumors, indicating that GBP2 does not influence tumor progression in the absence of adaptive immunity (Fig. S5C). This finding suggests that GBP2 may exert its antitumor function through modulating adaptive immune responses, particularly CD8⁺ T cell–mediated cytotoxicity. To assess the contribution of GBP2 to T cell–mediated tumor control, OVA‑specific CD8+ (OT‑1) T cells were adoptively transferred into mice bearing either control or GBP2−/− B16‑OVA tumors. OT‑1 transfer effectively suppressed the growth of control tumor growth; however, this effect was markedly diminished in GBP2−/− tumors (Fig. 2A, B). These findings suggest that GBP2 is essential for optimal CD8+ T‑cell–mediated tumor rejection, prompting evaluation of its role in ICB efficacy.

To this end, mice bearing GBP2−/− or sgCtrl B16-OVA tumors were treated with anti-PD-L1 blockade. GBP2 deficiency significantly reduced the antitumor efficacy of anti–PD‑L1 therapy compared to sgCtrl tumors (Fig. 2C, D). Similar results were observed in GBP2‑knockout MC38 tumors, in which GBP2 loss attenuated the response to combined OT‑1 transfer and anti–PD‑L1 treatment (Fig. S5D–H). These data indicate that GBP2 sensitizes tumor cells to CD8+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity, thereby enhancing ICB efficacy in vivo.

Considering that CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) eliminate tumor cells through multiple cell death pathways, we next sought to identify which CTL‑dependent cell death pathways are influenced by GBP2. OT-1 cells were co-cultured with GBP2oe B16-OVA cells in the presence of pathway‑specific inhibitors. Notably, treatment with the ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin‑1 (Fer‑1) significantly attenuated OT‑1-induced cytotoxicity in GBP2oe tumor cells, whereas inhibitors of pan‑caspases (emricasan), necroptosis (necrostatin‑1), or pyroptosis (disulfiram) had no effect (Fig. 2E). Consistently, GSEA revealed a strong positive correlation between GBP2 expression and ferroptosis signatures (Figs. 2F and S6A–E). These findings indicate that GBP2 facilitates CTL-mediated ferroptosis in tumor cells.

To further confirm this association, we measured lipid ROS—a hallmark of ferroptosis—in B16‑OVA tumors. GBP2 knockout tumors from both OT‑1 transfer and anti-PD-L1 treatment groups exhibited reduced lipid ROS levels relative to sgCtrl tumors (Figs. 2G, H and S6F, G). In vitro, GBP2 overexpression enhanced OT-1–induced cytotoxicity and intracellular lipid ROS, effects that were reversed by Fer-1 (Fig. 2I, J). Together, these results demonstrate that GBP2 promotes CTL‑induced ferroptosis and thereby enhances the antitumor efficacy of ICB therapy.

We next investigated the upstream signals through which GBP2 promotes ferroptosis. Given the known role of CD8⁺ T cell secreted cytokines in ICB-induced tumor cell death25, we measured IFN-γ and TNF-α levels in tumors with or without anti–PD‑L1 treatment. Under basal conditions, GBP2 loss had no effect on cytokine levels. At day 7 of anti–PD‑L1 therapy, both IFN-γ and TNF-α showed moderate increases in treated tumors, regardless of GBP2 status (Figs. 2K and S6H). Strikingly, in the late phase of treatment (Day 14), cytokine levels were markedly elevated in control tumors, whereas this increase was blunted in GBP2-deficient tumors, suggesting that GBP2 supports the sustained release of T cell–derived cytokines during late-phase ICB response (Figs. 2K and S6H).

To dissect which cytokine mediates the GBP2-dependent cell death, we co-cultured GBP2-overexpressing tumor cells with OT-1 cells lacking IFN-γ, TNF-α, or perforin. Loss of IFN-γ—but not TNF-α or perforin, abrogated OT‑1-mediated killing of GBP2oe tumor cells (Fig. 2L). These results support previous findings that IFN-γ can trigger ferroptosis in tumor cells and suggest that GBP2 may act within this pathway6,26. Thus, we performed in vivo neutralization experiments. GBP2 overexpression enhanced both anti-PD‑L1 efficacy and lipid ROS accumulation, effects that were completely abolished by anti-IFN‑γ monoclonal antibody treatment, confirming the dependence on IFN-γ signaling (Figs. 2M and S6I). Together, these data suggest that GBP2 acts as a general amplifier of CD8+ T cell–mediated cytotoxicity rather than an ICB-specific effector. GBP2 deficiency attenuated OT-1–driven tumor control even in the absence of PD-L1 blockade, highlighting its fundamental role in IFN-γ–dependent ferroptotic killing of tumor cells. Thus, GBP2 represents a core mediator of T cell cytotoxicity that potentiates the therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade.

GBP2 promotes tumor ferroptosis through STAT1/SLC7A11

We next sought to elucidate the molecular mechanism by which GBP2 regulates IFN-γ-induced ferroptosis. Long-chain-fatty-acid-CoA ligase 4 (ACSL4) is a well-established determinant of ferroptosis27, however, GBP2 depletion did not significantly alter ACSL4 expression (Fig. S7A). The cystine/glutamate antiporter system Xc−, consisting of the light-chain subunit (SLC7A11) and the heavy-chain subunit (SLC3A2), mediates extracellular cystine uptake for antioxidant glutathione (GSH) synthesis, thereby limiting lipid peroxidation and suppressing ferroptosis28,29. To explore whether system Xc− participates in GBP2-mediated ferroptosis regulation in melanoma cells, we examined the expression of its subunits. Compared with sgCtrl cells, sgGBP2 cells displayed a marked attenuation of IFN-γ-induced downregulation of SLC7A11 (Fig. 3A), whereas SLC3A2 expression remained unaffected by GBP2 deletion (Fig. S7B). In situ multi-color immunofluorescence staining of clinical melanoma samples revealed that tumors with high GBP2 expression exhibited lower SLC7A11 levels (Fig. 3B).

To determine whether GBP2 regulates ferroptosis via SLC7A11, we silenced SLC7A11 expression in GBP2−/− cells using siRNA (Fig. S7C and Supplementary Table 2). Upon treatment with the ferroptosis inducer RSL3, SLC7A11 knockdown restored the lipid ROS levels that were reduced by GBP2 deficiency in IFN-γ–primed B16-OVA cells (Fig. 3C). Similarly, GBP2 knockout markedly increased intracellular GSH content and cell viability—effects that were reversed by SLC7A11 silencing (Fig. 3D). In vivo, SLC7A11 overexpression significantly blunted the tumor-suppressive effect of GBP2 overexpression, reduced intratumoral levels of lipid ROS, and abolished its ability to potentiate ICB efficacy (Figs. 3E, F and S7D).

We then investigated the upstream mechanism by which GBP2 represses SLC7A11. Previous studies have implicated the STAT1 signaling pathway in SLC7A11 transcriptional regulation30. We therefore assessed whether GBP2 modulates SLC7A11 expression through STAT1 activation in melanoma. As anticipated, GBP2 depletion markedly reduced phosphorylated STAT1 (p-STAT1) levels in B16-OVA and A375 cells (Fig. 3G). Immunofluorescence imaging and nuclear–cytoplasmic fractionation following IFN-γ stimulation further demonstrated impaired nuclear translocation of p-STAT1 in GBP2−/− cells (Fig. 3H). STAT1 is a central regulator of antitumor immunity, orchestrating key ICB response pathways, including MHC-I antigen presentation, checkpoint ligand expression, and cytotoxic lymphocyte (CD8+ T/NK cell) recognition25. To assess whether STAT1-dependent functions were altered by GBP2 deletion, we examined MHC-I levels in B16-OVA and MC38-OVA cells using the PresentER system, which constitutively co-overexpresses OVA and MHC-I components via peptide/MHC complexes31. As a result, these cells constitutively overexpress both OVA antigen and MHC-I molecules, eliminating the possibility that reduced immunotherapy efficacy in the GBP2-knockout context is due to altered MHC-I presentation. Flow cytometry confirmed comparable MHC-I expression between sgCtrl and sgGBP2 cells (Fig. S7E, F). We next assessed PD-L1 expression. Western blot analysis of sgGBP2 cells revealed no significant difference between sgCtrl and sgGBP2 cells under basal or IFN-γ–stimulated conditions (Fig. S7G). To evaluate potential changes in immune recognition, we employed FucoID technology, which quantifies cell-cell interactions via interaction-dependent fucosyl-biotinylation32. No significant difference in CD8+ T/NK cell–tumor cell interaction frequency was detected between sgCtrl and sgGBP2 groups (Fig. S7H). These findings support that while GBP2 modulates STAT1 activation, it does not affect MHC-I expression, PD-L1 levels, or direct lymphocyte–tumor cell interactions in these models.

Based on these findings, we hypothesize that the STAT1/SLC7A11 axis mediates GBP2-driven ferroptosis. STAT1 has been reported to bind to the SLC7A11 promoter, repressing its transcription6. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) qPCR demonstrated that GBP2 loss abrogated IFN-γ–induced STAT1 binding to the transcription start site of SLC7A11 in B16-OVA and A375 cells (Fig. S7I). More strikingly, STAT1 knockout in GBP2oe B16-OVA cells abolished the increase in lipid ROS, leading to accelerated tumor growth (Figs. 3I–K and S7J). To exclude off-target effects, GBP2 re-expression in GBP2−/− B16-OVA cells significantly rescued SLC7A11 expression and STAT1 phosphorylation (Fig. S7K). Furthermore, enforced GBP2 expression of GBP2 in GBP2-deficient tumor cells restored lipid ROS accumulation and reinstated sensitivity to anti-PD-L1 in vivo (Fig. S7L, M). Together, these results demonstrate that GBP2 promotes ferroptosis by regulating the STAT1/SLC7A11 axis.

GBP2 undergoes phase separation to form condensates

Next, we investigated how GBP2 regulates the STAT1–SLC7A11 axis to promote ferroptosis. Recent studies have implicated phase separation as a critical mechanism triggering ferroptosis, with IFN-γ shown to induce phase separation of key proteins at high concentrations12,13,33,34. Given that GBP2 is an interferon-stimulated gene and that our results demonstrated GBP2 sensitizes tumor cells to IFN-γ-induced ferroptosis, we hypothesized that GBP2 might form biomolecular condensates via phase separation. To test this, we first analyzed the amino acid sequence of the GBP2 protein using the Predictor of Natural Disordered Regions (PONDR)35, which identified residues 436–579 (GBP2436–579) as an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (Fig. 4A). To visualize of GBP2 condensates, we generated B16-OVA and A375 cells with a mCherry tag knocked in at the C terminus of endogenous GBP2. Upon IFN-γ stimulation, endogenous GBP2 formed prominent droplet-like condensates that exhibited fusion and aggregation over time (Figs. 4B, C and S8A, B). We also assessed the dynamic properties of these condensates using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), observing >60% fluorescence recovery within approximately 2 min, indicative of liquid-like mobility (Figs. 4D and S8C). To validate our FRAP methodology, glycogen condensates served as a positive control and mCherry alone as a negative control36,37. Glycogen displayed rapid fluorescence recovery, consistent with known liquid-like dynamics (Fig. S8D), whereas mCherry showed negligible recovery, confirming its non-condensing behavior (Fig. S8E). These controls substantiate the dynamic and fluid nature of GBP2 condensates.

Moreover, treatment with 1,6-hexanediol (1,6-HD), which disrupts liquid–liquid phase separation by interfering with hydrophobic interactions, effectively abolished GBP2 puncta formation (Figs. 4E and S9A). To define the role of the IDR, we generated a deletion mutant lacking residues 436–579 (ΔIDR) in the mCherry-GBP2 construct and expressed it in B16-OVA and A375 cells. Considering the potential destabilization effect of removing this segment, recombinant full-length (FL) and ΔIDR GBP2 proteins were purified from E. coli, with Coomassie staining confirming proper folding of the ΔIDR mutant (Fig. S9B). In GBP2−/− B16-OVA cells transfected with FL or ΔIDR constructs, treatments with proteasomal (MG132), autophagic (BafA1), or lysosomal (chloroquine) inhibitors did not significantly affect GBP2 expression levels (Fig. S9C). Importantly, deletion of GBP2436–579 completely abolished condensate formation (Figs. 4F and S9D). Collectively, these data demonstrate that GBP2 forms the dynamic and reversible phase-separated condensates through its intrinsically disordered region, a property likely integral to its function in regulating ferroptosis.

GBP2 condensates retains SHP1 to protect STAT1 activation to promote ferroptosis

Previous studies have reported that the biomolecular condensates formed via phase separation can spatially restrict protein functions, including nuclear regulation or protein–proteins interactions38. To further elucidate whether GBP2 phase separation facilitates ferroptosis, we performed mass spectrometry to identify GBP2-interacting proteins. As a result, SHP1, a known phosphatase involved in dephosphorylating STAT1 in the IFN-γ signaling pathway39, was detected in GBP2-immunoprecipitates (Fig. 5A). This interaction was validated at both endogenous and exogenous levels by co-immunoprecipitation assays (Figs. 5B and S9E). Functionally, SHP1 knockdown in GBP2−/− cells substantially restored STAT1 phosphorylation and further suppressed SLC7A11 expression (Figs. 5C, S9F and Supplementary Table 2). We hypothesized that GBP2 modulates SHP1 activity through phase separation. Confocal microscopy revealed that GBP2 and SHP1 co-localize within droplet-like condensates in IFN-γ–treated B16-OVA cells, supporting a spatial sequestration model (Fig. 5D).

To investigate the functional relevance of GBP2-SHP1 condensates, we compared full-length GBP2 (FL) with the IDR deletion mutant in GBP2−/− cells. The ΔIDR mutant exhibited diminished IFN-γ–induced phase-separated compartments, accompanied by reduced STAT1 tyrosine phosphorylation and impaired nuclear translocation (Figs. 5E, F and S9G). Correspondingly, IDR deletion led to decreased lipid ROS levels and elevated intracellular GSH upon RSL3 treatment (Fig. S9H, I). Co-immunoprecipitation experiments further demonstrated direct SHP1–STAT1 binding, which was significantly enhanced in GBP2 knockout cells (Fig. S9J). High-resolution imaging confirmed the endogenous co-localization of GBP2 and SHP1 condensates, indicating that GBP2 physically sequesters SHP1 under physiological conditions (Fig. 5G). These findings support our central hypothesis that GBP2 condensates function as spatial regulators by enriching and isolating SHP1. To dissect this mechanism in vitro, we purified recombinant GBP2, SHP1, JAK2, and STAT1 proteins from E. coli, 293T, and Sf9 systems. Pre-formed GBP2 condensates were incubated with SHP1 before assessing STAT1 phosphorylation. Without GBP2 condensates, p-STAT1 levels rapidly decreased due to SHP1-mediated dephosphorylation. In contrast, the presence of GBP2 condensates preserved STAT1 phosphorylation, indicating effective SHP1 sequestration and impaired phosphatase activity (Fig. 5H). Similar results were observed with the ΔIDR mutant, which failed to form condensates and hence could not sequester SHP1 (Fig. 5I). Furthermore, fusion of GBP2 with a hydrophilic maltose-binding protein (MBP) tag to reduce self-association disrupted condensate formation and SHP1 sequestration in vitro, resulting in decreased STAT1 phosphorylation compared to wild-type GBP2 (Fig. 5J). Collectively, these results demonstrate that GBP2 phase separation is essential for sequestering SHP1 and sustaining STAT1 signaling, robustly supporting our claims regarding the functional role of phase separation.

In vivo, introducing GBP2436-579 significantly impaired GBP2-FL-mediated lipid ROS accumulation, accelerated tumor growth, and attenuated anti–PD-L1 therapy efficacy (Fig. 5K, L). Comparable results were observed in OT-1 adoptive cell therapy models (Fig. S10K–M). Co-immunoprecipitation from PD-L1-treated tumors revealed enhanced STAT1-SHP1 binding and decreased STAT1 phosphorylation in GBP2-ΔIDR tumors (Fig. 5M). Furthermore, in vivo phase separation could observe aggregation foci under immunofluorescence36. We performed immunofluorescence staining on these tumor specimens and visualized distinct GBP2 aggregate foci in GBP2-FL tumors following anti-PD-L1 treatment, whereas such structures were absent in GBP2-ΔIDR tumors (Fig. 5N). These findings convincingly demonstrate that CTL-secreted IFN-γ promotes GBP2 phase separation, facilitating SHP1 sequestration, which sustains STAT1 activation, represses SLC7A11 transcription, and induces ferroptosis.

GBP2 promotes the intratumoral CD8+ T cell infiltration through enhancing the immunogenicity of ferroptotic cells

Next, we aimed to investigate the impact of GBP2 on the tumor immune microenvironment (TME) under ICB therapy. We first analyzed the correlation between GBP2 and TME in melanoma patients using the ssGSEA algorithm to estimate the abundance of 28 immune cell types across six cohorts. GBP2 expression was strongly associated with an inflamed immune microenvironment, showing a significant positive correlation primarily with CD8⁺ T cells (Fig. S10A). To validate these findings experimentally, we performed flow cytometry on tumor-infiltrating leukocytes from anti‑PD‑L1–treated sgGBP2 and sgCtrl tumors. Applying the established gating strategies40, we quantified the major immune subsets, including CD8⁺ T cells, CD4⁺ T cells, NK cells, B cells, neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and dendritic cells (DCs) (Fig. S10B). Anti-PD-L1 treatment significantly increased the proportions of CD8⁺ T cells, CD4⁺ T cells, NK cells and B cells. Critically, GBP2 deletion substantially reduced infiltration of CD8⁺ T cells regardless of PD-L1 treatment, while CD4⁺ T cells, DCs, B cells, NK cells, macrophages, and neutrophils were unaffected (Fig. 6A). Similarly, flow cytometry revealed that CD8+ OT-1 cell was markedly lower in GBP2-/- tumors compared to controls (Fig. 6B, C). Given the pivotal role of CD8+ T cells in antitumor immunity, we depleted CD8+ T cells in vivo and observed that tumor growth in the oeGBP2 group was increased (Fig. 6D), underscoring the dependence of GBP2-mediated tumor suppression on CD8⁺ T cells. Furthermore, flow cytometric analysis of CD8⁺ T cell activation markers showed that GBP2 ablation markedly attenuated IFN-γ⁺ and TNF-α⁺ CD8⁺ T cell frequencies (Fig. 6E). Analysis of a single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE115978) from 32 melanoma patients using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) identified 25 cell clusters into 8 major immune cell types based on canonical marker expression (Fig. S10C). Notably, the five patients with highest GBP2 expression exhibited significantly increased CD8⁺ T cell infiltration (Figs. 6F and S10D). Immunofluorescence staining of further corroborated GBP2-FL tumors following anti-PD-L1 harbored greater CD8⁺ T cell infiltration (Fig. 6G). Collectively, these data demonstrate that GBP2 shapes an immunostimulatory TME, potentiating CD8+ T cell-mediated antitumor immunity.

Recent studies have revealed that ferroptotic tumor cells release damage associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), conferring an immunogenic cell death (ICD)-like phenotype41. Importantly, ICD promotes the recruitment and activation of DCs, which facilitate tumor antigen presentation to CTL, enhancing CD8+ T cell infiltration and activation42. Since GBP2 significantly potentiates CTL-induced ferroptosis, we hypothesized that GBP2 promotes CTL-mediated killing by triggering the ICD feature in ferroptotic tumor cells. To test this, we measured levels of the DAMP high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) in tumor tissues from mouse models. ELISA revealed that GBP2 deficiency significantly reduced HMGB1 release under both anti-PD-L1 and OT-1 therapies (Fig. S11A). Concordantly, GBP2−/− tumors exhibited decreased expression of DC maturation markers, including the co-stimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 (Fig. S11B). Analysis of single-cell data also showed elevated CD86 expression in patients with high GBP2 expression (Fig. S11C). Deletion of STAT1 in GBP2-overexpressing tumors significantly reduced HMGB1 levels, while SLC7A11 overexpression rescued the GBP2-induced HMGB1 upregulation (Fig. S11D, E). Furthermore, HMGB1 knockout in GBP2-overexpressing B16-OVA cells accelerated tumor growth in vivo, accompanied by diminished CD8⁺ OT-1 T cell infiltration and reduced CD80/CD86 expression (Fig. S11F–I). Together, these results suggest that GBP2 enhances the immunogenicity of ferroptotic tumor cells through HMGB1 release, thereby promoting CD8⁺ T cell infiltration in melanoma.

GBP2 facilitates ICB response in tumor patients

Next, we sought to validate the correlation between GBP2 expression and ICB response in human melanoma. We compared three established predictive signatures for ICB response: T cell inflamed expression profile (GEP), innate anti-PD-1 resistance (IPRES) and immuno-predictive score (IMPRES) signatures43–45. Higher enrichment scores of all three signatures were observed in the high GBP2 expression group across multiple melanoma cohorts (Figs. 7A and S12A–D). Using SubMap analysis to compare GBP2 expression profiles with a published melanoma immunotherapy dataset46, the high GBP2 group demonstrated significant similarity to the PD-1 responder group across five cohorts (Figs. 7B and S12E–H). Additionally, we analyzed a cohort comprising pre-treatment (PRE) biopsies taken prior to immunotherapy (n=73), and early during treatment (EDT) samples (7–14 days post-treatment initiation, n=18) (Supplementary Dataset 2). PRE samples with high GBP2 expression exhibited markedly improved clinical responses to ICB compared to low GBP2 samples. Conversely, patients with high SLC7A11 expression showed increased ICB resistance (Figs. 7C and S13A). More importantly, stratifying PRE samples by GBP2 and SLC7A11 expression yielded three groups: group 1 (high GBP2/low SLC7A11), group 2 (low GBP2/low SLC7A11 or high GBP2/high SLC7A11), and group 3 (low GBP2/high SLC7A11). Group 1 displayed the highest percentage of complete or partial responses (CR/PR), while group 3 had the lowest (Fig. 7D). Due to limited EDT samples, direct comparison revealed elevated GBP2 expression in ICB responders versus non-responders (Fig. S13B). Survival analyses indicated that among ICB-treated patients, the high GBP2 group had superior prognosis compared to the low GBP2 group, whereas high SLC7A11 predicted poorer outcomes (Figs. 7E and S13C). Moreover, group 1 exhibited the most favorable survival outcome, followed by group 2, with group 3 demonstrating the shortest OS (Fig. 7F). Similar patterns of elevated GBP2 expression in ICB responders were observed in metastatic urothelial carcinoma and non-small cell lung cancer cohorts47,48, where high GBP2 expression also predicted better prognosis (Fig. S13D, E).

To explore spatial heterogeneity, we analyzed spatial transcriptomics data from a hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) dataset, dividing tissue slices into malignant, boundary, and non-malignant regions (Figs. 7G and S13F). Responders exhibited higher GBP2 and lower SLC7A11 expression in malignant areas, accompanied by increased CD8⁺ T cell infiltration, compared to non-responders (Figs. 7H and S13G). Finally, immunohistochemistry (IHC) of melanoma samples validated that high GBP2 expression correlated with reduced SLC7A11 levels (Fig. 7I). Together, these findings indicate that elevated GBP2 predicts improved OS and better ICB response in tumor patients.
paper_content.methods:
Humans samples and animals
All melanoma cases were pathologically confirmed by two independent pathologists, and only treatment-naïve samples from patients without other malignancies were included. Only clinical samples collected in excess of those needed for diagnostic and therapeutic procedures were used for research. All participants provided written informed consent for the collection and subsequent analysis of their samples and clinical data. Twelve resected human melanoma tissues were obtained from patients at Zhongnan Hospital of Wuhan University. The information of patients is shown in Supplementary Table 3. Six-week-old female and male C57BL/6 mice and NOD. Cg-Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice were purchased from the Hubei BIONT Biological Technology Co., LTD. OT-1 mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory. Sex specific differences were not investigated as the study focused on general treatment efficacy rather than sex-related outcomes.

Animal model and treatment protocols
C57BL/6 mice were subcutaneously injected with sgCtrl and GBP2−/− B16-OVA or MC38-OVA cells (1×106/ml). When the tumors had grown to 125 mm3, the C57BL/6 mice were randomized into different groups. The anti-PD-L1 antibody (200 μg per mouse) and IgG isotype were administered intraperitoneally every 3 days until the end of the observation period.

For CTL killing in vivo, OT-1 cells are first isolated and enriched. In detail, after grinding the spleen to obtain a single-cell suspension, the suspension was placed in 2 ml of red blood cell lysis buffer (Sigma Aldrich) for 1 min. Then, CD8+ OT-1 cells were purified using EasySep mouse CD8+ T Cell Isolation Kit (Stemcell). The CD8+ OT-1 cells were cultured at 2×106/ml in RPMI culture medium containing 2 nM OVA 257-264 (SIINFEKL), 10 ng/mL human recombinant IL-2, and 50 μM 2-mercaptoethanol. The cells were incubated at 37°C for 5 days. Finally, C57BL/6 mice were subcutaneously injected with cells as indicated. Enriched OT-1 cells (5×106/ml per mouse, every 7 days) were resuspended into 200 μl PBS and intravenously injected into tumor-bearing mice. All the tumor volume (mm3) was measured and calculated as follows: formula: V = a × b × b / 2.

Cell culture and reagents
A human melanoma cell line (A375), mouse melanoma cell line (B16-OVA), mouse colon carcinoma cell line (MC38-OVA) and human HEK 293T cells were obtained from the Cell Resource Centre of Peking Union Medical College (Beijing, China). All cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium (Hyclone, USA) with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco, Australia) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin at 37°C with 5% CO2. All cell lines were authenticated by short tandem repeat (STR) fingerprinting and tested to confirm no mycoplasma contamination and used in the experiments were within 20 passages. Human and murine recombinant IFN-γ were purchased from PeproTech. The in vivo murine anti-PD-L1 antibody (BE0101) and IgG isotype (BE0089) were purchased from BioXCell. The ferroptosis agonizts RSL3 (S8155) and inhibitor ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1, S7243) were purchased from Selleck.

CRISPR–Cas9-mediated genome editing
The CRISPR/Cas9 based on pX459 plasmid was constructed. The guide RNA sequences were listed in Supplementary Table 1. For CRISPR/Cas9 plasmid transfection, B16-OVA and A375 cells were transfected according to instructions for the lipofectamine 2000 and sorted by puromycin to acquire a monoclonal cell line. Finally, the GBP2−/−, HMGB1−/− and STAT1−/− cells were identified via western blotting and cultured for further analysis.

Stable overexpressing cell line construction
To generate stable GBP2 overexpressing cells, Pspax2, pVSV-G and constructed Plvx-IRES-Puro or empty vector were transfected into HEK 293T cells using lipofectamine 2000. The supernatants containing viruses were added in B16-OVA with multiplicity of infection (MOI) at 5:1 and with the concentration of Polybrene at 8 μg/ml and the infection lasted for 12 h. After 48 h infection, puromycin was added to cells and the cells were treated with concentration at 1.5 μg/ml. The treatment lasted for 3 days, and the cells were kept in puromycin in half of the concentration for stable selection.

Lipid ROS detection
For the detection of lipid ROS in vivo, tumor tissues were chopped, ground, and filtered to form a single-cell suspension. Then, the density gradient centrifugation (Ficoll, Sigma-Aldrich) was used to pre-enrichment. Finally, the cell pellet was stained with anti-CD45 (30-F11) and anti-OVA 257–264 -H2Kb (25-D1.16) antibodies. Afterwards, 5 μM BODIPY-C11 (D3861, Thermo Fisher Scientific) staining were performed and incubated at 37°C for 30 min. The signal of oxidized C11 was immediately analyzed using flow cytometry.

For the detection of lipid ROS in vitro, B16-OVA cells (2×104/ml) co-cultured with activated OT-1 (B16-OVA:OT-1 ratio of 5:1) for 24 h followed by treatment with 10 μM Fer-1 for an additional 24 h. OT-1 cells were removed via gently washing several times with PBS. Then, the 5 μM C11-BODIPY 581/591 working solution was added and incubated with cells for 30 min in the incubator. Ready-to-use DAPI staining solution (C1005, Beyotime, China) was used to stain the nuclei for 5 min. After washing twice, the cells were covered with HBSS, and the images of oxidized C11 (wavelength 505–550 nm) were captured using a fluorescence microscope.

Cell viability detection
Cell viability was measured using a CellTiter-Glo Luminescent Cell Viability Assay kit (Promega), which is based on the luciferase reaction to measure the amount of ATP from viable cells. The amount of ATP in the cells correlates with cell viability.

Western blot
First, total protein fractions of melanoma cells were obtained using NP40 lysis buffer (Beyotime, China). The BCA kits (Beyotime, China) were used to determine the concentration of the protein fractions. Then, 30 μg of protein from each group was run on a 10% SDS-PAGE gel and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes (Millipore, USA). The PVDF membranes were blocked with 5% fat-free milk and incubated overnight at 4°C with the appropriate primary antibodies: GBP2 (11854-1-AP, Proteintech, USA), p-STAT1 (#9167, CST, USA), STAT1 (#14994, CST, USA), SLC7A11 (#98051, CST, USA), SLC3A2 (15193-1-AP, Proteintech, USA), ACSL4 (22401-1-AP, Proteintech, USA), PD-L1 (17952-1-AP, Proteintech, USA), HMGB1 (10829-1-AP, Proteintech, USA), SHP1 (24546-1-AP, Proteintech, USA), and GAPDH (10494-1-AP, Proteintech, USA). Finally, enhanced chemiluminescence reagents (Thermo, USA) were applied to detect the bands after incubation with secondary antibody (GB23303, Servicebio, China).

Flow cytometric analysis of tumor-infiltrating immune cells
B16-OVA cells were subcutaneously injected into mice, which were then treated with anti–PD-L1 antibody as described in the animal section. On day 21 after treatment, tumors were harvested, weighed, mechanically minced, and digested with collagenase IV (2 mg/mL; Sigma-Aldrich) and DNase I (50 μg/mL; Sigma-Aldrich) for 1 h. The resulting cell suspension was triturated and passed through a 70 μm cell strainer to obtain a single-cell suspension. Cells were blocked with anti-mouse CD16/32 antibody (BioLegend) and stained with the indicated antibodies on ice for 30 min. Live/Dead Aqua dye (1:1,000; Thermo Fisher Scientific) was added together with surface antibodies to exclude dead cells. After washing, cells were fixed and permeabilized using the Foxp3/transcription factor staining buffer set (eBioscience) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, blocked with mouse and rat serum, and then stained with intracellular antibodies. All stained cells were analyzed on an Attune NxT systems and the data was analyzed with FlowJo version 10 software.

ELISA assay
Cytokine production in the homogenate supernatant from tumor tissue was quantified by ELISA kits (R&D Systems) according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

Protein expression, purification, and in vitro kinase assay
To obtain recombinant wild-type (WT) proteins, their corresponding mutants, MBP-tagged, or fluorescent GBP2 proteins, E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells harboring the respective constructs (pGEX vector) were cultured in LB medium supplemented with 50 μg/mL kanamycin. Protein expression was induced overnight at 18°C with 0.1 mM IPTG once the OD600 reached 0.8. Cells were lysed in a buffer containing 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, 1 mM DTT, 1 mM PMSF, and 1 mg/mL lysozyme. Fusion proteins were purified by affinity chromatography using glutathione-Sepharose resin (GE Healthcare Life Sciences, USA). The purity of the purified GBP2 was evaluated by electrophoresis on a 10% polyacrylamide gel, followed by Coomassie Blue staining and immunoblotting. Human SHP1 was expressed in E. coli BL21 (DE3) cells using an N-terminal strep-tag construct. Protein expression was induced with IPTG at 18°C overnight, and the protein was purified by Ni2+-affinity chromatography followed by size-exclusion chromatography. JAK2 was expressed in HEK293T cells by transient transfection, and the protein was isolated from cell lysates using anti-FLAG affinity resin and further purified by gel filtration. STAT1 was produced in Sf9 insect cells using the baculovirus expression system, and purified through Ni2+ affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography.

For in vitro kinase assays, purified STAT1 was incubated with JAK2 in kinase buffer (50 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 10 mM MgCl₂, 1 mM DTT, 100 μM ATP) at 30°C. When indicated, GBP2 or SHP1 was added after phosphorylation to examine dephosphorylation. Reactions were terminated by adding SDS sample buffer and analyzed by SDS‑PAGE and immunoblotting with phospho-specific antibodies.

In vitro T cell killing assay
Differentially labeled, B16-OVA cells were seeded into 12-well plates in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS. After 24 h, the medium was replaced with RPMI containing 10% FBS and preactivated OT-I T cells at the indicated effector-to-target ratios. After 24 h of co-culture, tumor cells were harvested and analyzed by flow cytometry to assess cell viability.

In vitro and cellular phase separation assay
Phase separation of recombinant wild-type or MBP-tagged mCherry‑GBP2 proteins with recombinant GFP‑tagged SHP1 was examined in LLPS buffer (40 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, and 1.25% PEG8000). Protein mixtures were gently mixed and incubated at room temperature, and 10 μL of the reaction was placed on a glass slide, covered with a coverslip, and immediately imaged using a confocal microscope.

Generation of endogenously tagged GBP2-mCherry cell line
CRISPR–Cas9 with a single guide RNA (sgRNA) targeting the endogenous GBP2 locus was used to insert a mCherry sequence immediately before the stop codon in B16-OVA. An oligonucleotide encoding this sgRNA (TGAAGCAAAACAAATCGTCT) was cloned into pX330, which also encodes Cas9 (Addgene no. 42230). Six hundred thousand B16-OVA cells were seeded and transfected with 0.5 μg pX330/sgRNA vector and 1 μg repair template, consisting of mCherry flanked by 800-base pair (bp) homology arms using lipo2000. One week later, mCherry-positive cells were collected by sorting and single-cell clones were generated. Successful targeting was verified by sequencing.

Live cell imaging
Cells were grown on poly-l-lysine-treated no. 1.5 cover glass chambers (Lab-Tek) for 24 h. Before imaging, culture medium was replaced with RPM-1640 (Thermo Fisher) supplemented with 10% FBS and 1× GlutaMAX (Thermo Fisher). Cells were imaged with a Nikon A1R+ confocal microscope with a 60× oil objective and a Nikon A1 camera equipped with a heated stage (37°C) and 5% CO2 environment.

Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching
FRAP was performed using a Nikon A1R+ microscope with a 488-nm or 561-nm laser. For FRAP experiments on GBP2 condensates in living cells, the entire punctum, typically less than 1 μm in diameter, was photobleached using 70% laser power, before time-lapse imaging. Fluorescence intensity in the photobleached region was measured using ImageJ and values were normalized to pre-bleach time points.

Coimmunoprecipitation (CoIP)
Total protein fractions were collected for CoIP with indicated antibody according to the manufacturer’s protocol using an IP/CoIP kit (Absin, China). In brief, 293T, A375, and B16-OVA cells were lysed with IP buffer (P0013J, Beyotime, China) containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors for 45 min at 4°C. The cell lysates were precleared with protein A/G-agarose beads for 1 h and then incubated with IgG, indicated antibody, overnight at 4°C with continuous inversion. The cell lysates were precipitated with protein A/G-agarose beads for 4 h and then the immunoprecipitated beads were washed five times the following day. Bound proteins were eluted and subjected to immunoblot analysis with indicated antibodies.

siRNA transfection
The human and mouse SHP1 and SLC7A11 siRNAs were purchased from Ribobio (Guangzhou, China). B16-OVA and A375 cells was transfected with siRNA using lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen, USA). Scramble siRNA was used as a control. Sequences of siRNAs were listed in the Supplementary Table 2.

Chromatin immunoprecipitation assay (ChIP)
A Sonication ChIP kit (Abclonal, China) was used to perform the ChIP assay according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, 1×107 cells were cross-lined with 1% formaldehyde for 8 min at room temperature. Then, fixed cells were harvested, lysed, and sonicated on ice with several pulses and incubated for 30 s on ice between pulses. The sheared chromatin fragments were immunoprecipitated with antibodies against STAT1 (5 μl per 1 mg total protein) and rabbit IgG (2 μl per 1 mg total protein). After elution and decross-linking, the enriched DNA fragments were purified by universal DNA purification kit (DP214, TIANGEN). The primer sequences used for ChIP-qPCR are listed in the Supplementary Table 4.

Multiplex immunofluorescence analysis and IHC analysis
Multiplex immunofluorescence staining was obtained using PANO 3-plex IHC kit (Panovue, Beijing, China). The primary antibodies of GBP2 (27299-1-AP, Proteintech, USA), SLC7A11 (ab307601; Abcam, USA), and CD8A (A11856, ABclonal, USA) were sequentially applied, followed by horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody incubation and tyramide signal amplification (TSA). The slides were microwave-treated after each TSA operation. Nuclei were stained with DAPI after all the human antigens had been labeled. In addition, standard immunohistochemistry protocol was also performed using the above antibodies60.

Immunofluorescence
Collected cells were spun down onto a coverslip, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100. Fixed cells were blocked in 5% BSA and probed with anti-p-STAT1 (#9167, CST, USA) antibody in 5% BSA, followed by Alexa Fluor® 488 Goat anti-rabbit (ab150077, Abcam, USA) and the slides were further counterstained with DAPI and mounted for confocal analysis and the fluorescent image was observed under a fluorescent microscope.

The glutathione (GSH) assay
The reduced (GSH) assay kit (Nanjing Jiancheng) was used to quantitatively analyze the levels of intracellular GSH according to the supplier’s instructions.

Datasets collection
In this work, 7 independent melanoma cohorts were selected, including a total of 1076 melanoma patients: skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM) from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA); GSE6590461; GSE840162; GSE5945563; GSE318964; GSE11597865 and PRJEB2370966. The upper quartile fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped reads (FPKM-UQ) for SKCM were downloaded from the UCSC Xena browser (https://xenabrowser.net/datapages/). The PRJEB23709 cohort was obtained from the Tumor Immunotherapy Gene Expression Resource database (http://tiger.canceromics.org/#/download)67. The remaining five cohorts were all downloaded from the Gene Expression Omnibus database (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/). Detailed information of above datasets is shown in Supplementary Dataset 3.

Bioinformatic analysis
The relative abundance of 28 immune cell infiltration in each melanoma sample was quantified via ssGSEA (Supplementary Dataset 4)68,69. We used the “limma” R package to screen the differentially infiltrating cells in the tumors separated by median GBP2 expression (high versus low). An unsupervised subclass mapping method (SubMap) (GenePattern module ‘SubMap’) (https://cloud.genepattern.org) was used to identify common subgroups between independent cohorts despite their technical differences70. A melanoma dataset including anti-PD-1 and anti-CTLA4 therapy was applied to measure the similarity with high- and low-GBP2 groups in other melanoma datasets included in this study46. The spatial tumor microenvironment (SpatialTME) database was used to analyze the spatial transcriptome of one melanoma samples (https://www.spatialtme.yelab.site/#!/search/Visium/Melanoma_10x/Melanoma_IFStainedFFPE_CytAssist_10x)71. A spatial transcriptome dataset of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) containing ICB therapy was also used to validate our results72. For survival analysis, Kaplan–Meier survival curves and log-rank tests were used to evaluate the outcomes of melanoma patients in the with high- and low-GBP2 groups according to “survival” R package.

Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) and gene ontology (GO) functional annotation
GSEA was used to enrich the significant gene sets between the high- and low-GBP2 groups. The gene sets of “H.all.v7.4” were downloaded from the Molecular Signatures Database and used as the reference set to represent well-defined biological states or processes. Additionally, Gene Ontology (GO) functional enrichment analysis was performed using the DAVID database (https://david.ncifcrf.gov/)73. The GTP binding protein were collected from the GO term of GTP binding (GO: 0005525) according to the quickGO website (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/QuickGO/) (Supplementary Dataset 5).

Weighted gene coexpression network analysis (WGCNA)
First, raw data of GSE8401 were preprocessed with RMA background correction, log2 transformation, and quantile normalization, and then the median-polish probeset summarization was applied through the “Affy” R package74. The probes were annotated through the “hgu133a.db” R package. GSE8401 was assessed by sample clustering according to the distance between different samples in Pearson’s correlation matrices. Using a cutoff height of 60, no samples were removed (Fig. S1A). Genes were filtered by median absolute deviation (MAD) since low-expressed or non-varying genes usually represent noise. The “WGCNA” R package was used to construct a coexpression network according to the top 5000 genes sorted by MAD74,75. Then, we calculated the Pearson’s correlation matrices for all paired genes. A weighted adjacency matrix was further constructed using a power function a = |c |β (c = Pearson’s correlation between gene m and gene n; a = adjacency between gene m and gene n). β was a soft thresholding parameter that could emphasize strong correlations between genes and penalize weak correlations. The power of β = 6 was selected as a soft threshold to ensure a scale-free network (Fig. S1B–E). Moreover, the adjacency was transformed into a topological overlap matrix (TOM) that could measure the network connectivity of a gene and is defined as the sum of its adjacency with all other genes for network generation76. The average linkage hierarchical clustering was used to classify genes with similar expression profiles into different modules with a minimum gene group size of 3077. Finally, we used the module eigengenes (MEs) to identify gene modules of interest related to phenotype. MEs were deemed as the first principal component in the principal component analysis for each gene module, which summarizes the expression patterns of all genes into a single characteristic expression profile within a given module.

Statistical analysis and reproducibility
All experiments were performed at least three independent experiments. All results are shown as means ± SD. Comparisons between two unpaired groups were evaluated by two-tailed Student’s t test. Two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test and ANOVA with multiple comparisons were used to calculate P values. Correlations between groups were determined by Pearson’s correlation test. The numbers of samples and independent biological experimental repeats are indicated in the figures or figure legends. The P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The analysis was conducted using the GraphPad 8.0 software and R 4.1.3 software.

Ethical statement
The study was conducted in accordance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhongnan Hospital of Wuhan University (approval No. ZN2024028K). C57BL/6 mice, NOD. Cg-Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice and OT-1 mice, C57BL/6-Tg(TcraTcrb)1100Mjb/J were housed under specific pathogen free conditions. These animals were specific pathogen-free and maintained in 6 animals per group on a 12/12-h light/dark cycle at 20–26°C with around 40–70% humidity, and given ad libitum access to standard food and water. All procedures involving mice and research protocols were approved by the Experimental Animal Welfare Ethics Committee, Zhongnan Hospital of Wuhan University (approval No. ZN2024072) and the Ethics Committee of the Experimental Animal Care of Beijing Chest Hospital, Capital Medical University (approval No. XK-2025-059). The maximal tumor size permitted by the ethics committee is 1500 mm3. Throughout this study, this tumor size limit was strictly monitored and was not exceeded in any of the experimental animals.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript explores the role of GBP2 in immunogenic ferroptosis and ICB response in tumors, an intriguing and relevant topic in cancer immunotherapy. The authors provide a detailed analysis integrating bioinformatics, in vivo models, and molecular analyses to establish a link between GBP2, phase separation, and STAT1 activation in the tumor microenvironment. However, in some cases, the conclusions are based solely on correlations and require further validation to fully support the proposed model.
1. CRISPR/Cas9 Off-Target Effects: The use of CRISPR/Cas9 technology can lead to off-target mutations. How did the authors verify that the generated cell lines do not carry unintended genetic alterations? A proper validation should be included to ensure the accuracy of the reported data.
2. IFN-γ and Ferroptosis: The authors suggest that IFN-γ induces ferroptosis via GBP2; however, this is not supported by experimental data. To clarify this, cytokine levels should be measured in tumours derived from GBP2-/- and control cells (with or without ICB) to assess IFN-γ and other relevant cytokines in the tumour microenvironment. This would also help determine the inflammatory status in the presence or absence of GBP2 in the context of ICB. Additionally, in vivo IFN-γ blocking experiments should be performed to establish a functional link between GBP2 and IFN-γ.
3. FRAP Analysis: The FRAP data presented are incomplete. To fully characterize GBP2 phase separation properties, appropriate controls should be included, such as a protein known to form condensates and a protein known to remain solubilized. This comparison would help determine whether GBP2 phase separation follows a typical liquid-liquid phase separation behaviour.
4. GBP2ΔIDR and ICB Response: The authors demonstrate that GBP2ΔIDR reduces CD8+ OT-1 cytotoxicity; however, they do not assess whether GBP2 phase separation is required for ICB efficacy in vivo. A murine model with GBP2ΔIDR + anti-PD-L1 should be used to determine if GBP2 condensation is necessary for a successful ICB response.
5. Immune Infiltration Profiling: The authors suggest that GBP2 may modulate immune responses by promoting immunogenic cell death. Since this mechanism has significant implications for immune cells, a more comprehensive analysis of tumour-infiltrating leukocytes should be performed. This should not be limited to CD8+ T cells and DCs but should include a full leukocyte profile in mice transplanted with GBP2-/- and sgGBP2 tumour cells, with or without ICB therapy. Additionally, the authors should assess whether CD8+ T cells show increased activation in sgGBP2 tumours.
6. Manuscript Readability and Clarity: The manuscript should be carefully revised to improve clarity and readability. Lines 273-275 contain a sentence that appears incorrect and contradicts the data presented. Please revise this section for accuracy.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Summary:
Liu et al performed a weighted network correlation analysis of immune checkpoint blockade-treated patients and identified GBP2 as a potential driver of ICB response. They find that loss of GBP2 ablates PD-L1 response in mouse models and argue that GBP2 acts to enhance T-cell-mediated ferroptosis via modulation of SLCA11 in an IFN-dependent manner. They further argue that GBP2 forms phase-separated condensates that sequester SHP1 and thereby promote STAT1 phosphorylation and subsequent induction of SLCA11. They seek to validate this finding in patient cohorts and argue that GBP2 acts to support ferroptosis, immunogenicity cell death and HMGB1 expression.
Overall the group presents a large body of intriguing data. The finding that GBP2 modulates and supports IFNg / STAT1 signaling via phase separated sequestration of SHP1 is interesting. They separately show that GBP2 loss impairs ferroptosis and that this impairment can be overcome by SLCA11 knockdown. Each of these findings represents a meaningful contribution to the field and, in particular, the work supporting SHP1 sequestration by GBP2 seems to me to be a strength. That said, there are also some concerns with the paper as currently constructed.
Major Concerns:
There are some logical leaps that I worry are not fully justified by the data. For example, because loss of GBP2 affects STAT1 signaling and STAT signaling affects many pathways of immunotherapy response (not least, MHC-I expression, expression of checkpoint ligands, CD8+ T cell and NK cell recognition), I am not sure that the data connecting GBP2 with ferroptosis and the data connecting GBP2 with immunotherapy response are necessarily connected. The authors could strengthen this connection by testing whether SLCA11 overexpression in tumor cells ablates the in vivo GBP2 PD-L1 response phenotype they observe. I would also recommend evaluating alternative or complementary hypotheses by testing the expression of other IFN-stimulated genes such as MHC-I in GBP2 ko cell lines. Finally, the authors rely heavily on a single mouse model for in vivo studies and could benefit from repeating core findings (e.g. GBP2 sensitization to PD-L1) in an additional model to support its robustness.
I am additionally concerned about the potential for circular reasoning in the patient correlative studies: better clinical responses with GBP2, more immunogenic tumor cell death or more CD8+ T cells may not be all that surprising given that GBP2 is an ISG. Indeed, correlations are presented between IFN-signatures (composed of ISGs) and GBP2. In this case it seems quite possible that cause and effect may be reversed– that GBP2 expression is the effect of ISG induction rather than the cause, as is claimed. By comparison, analysis could equally be conducted simply asking if IFN signaling in tumors correlates with CD8+ T cell infiltration or whether they respond better to immunotherapy–both well established observations in the field.
The manuscript would benefit from editing for grammar in several places and rewriting in some others. I did not, for the most part, try to enumerate grammar or style issues. However, examples include:
- Spelling and usage in the title: consider ‘promote’, not ‘promotes’; ‘sensitize’, not ‘sensitive’
- Consider referring to immune checkpoint blockade as simply ‘ICB’ rather than ‘the ICB’
- Line 79: consider ‘augments’, not ‘augment’, ‘limits’, not ‘limit’.
Specific Points:
- Please add quantitative axes for flow plots
- Fig 1: this analysis is generally correlational, which can lend to false positives. In particular, the authors ultimately correlate an ISG (GBP2) with a signatures for ISGs (e.g. IFNg signature). That said, this is probably ok in Fig 1, as the exercise is hypothesis-generating and sets up the rest of the work.
- Why is GBP2 considered a ‘combinatorial ICB treatment biomarker’ at the end of Fig 1, rather than simply a biomarker? Also, is it thought to be prognostic or predictive?
- Fig 2: although the statistics shown look very significant, the difference in tumor volume appears modest for Fig 2 A, C. Indeed, it appears that PD-L1 treatment was not particularly effective in this model. It is likely worth testing other models in which PD-L1 blockade is more effective to see if the phenotypes are reproducible / stronger there.
- Fig 3A: Please quantify Western blots if reporting significance.
- Fig 4: It would strengthen the conclusions to repeat at least some of these experiments in another cell line
- Fig 5K: It seems important to show expression and stability of the delta IDR GBP2 protein (unless I missed this data)– otherwise it may mis-fold or be unstable and effectively just knock the protein down.
- Is GBP2 genetically lost / selected against in tumors? The authors’ findings would predict that it should be, given that this is claimed to induce resistance to anti-tumor immunity in an immunogenic disease.
- Fig 3: Given the purported mechanism, It would be helpful to see whether overexpression of SLC7A11 obviates the effect of GBP2 knockout to prove that this is per se the mechanism of impaired tumor growth.
- The STAT1 ko result is already well known as a broad resistance mechanism for B16 tumors, and so may or may not be related to GBP2 biology here.
- Fig 3B: how many samples is this representative example drawn from?
- Fig 3E: Given that the authors argue that GBP2 limits STAT1 signaling, it should limit ISGs broadly. Do the authors therefore see lower MHC-I and PD-L1 expression in IFNg-stimulated GBP2 ko cells?
- Fig 5: It would be helpful to see co-localization of SHP1 and STAT1 or pSTAT1 together in the same images in GBP2 KO vs GBP2-expressing cells.
- Fig 6: HMGB1 is not particularly specific for ferroptotic death. Other IFN-dependent pathways of killing (ie most of them since IFN affects T cell recognition via MHC-I) could presumably be equally implicated here. Overexpressing SLC7A11 may provide stronger evidence than deletion of STAT1, which is a general way to suppress tumor response.
- Fig 7: many of these analyses may be confounded by the relationship of GBP2 as an ISG— independent of any role in supporting anti-tumor immunity, GBP2 should anyhow be associated with response: because responding patients have T cells that make IFNg.
- I did not see computational methods reported in the methods section.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript titled “Gbp2 condensate promote ferroptosis, sensitize anti-PD-L1 ICB in melanoma” investigates the role of Gbp2 in enhancing immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) in a mouse model. The authors propose that under IFN-γ stimulation, Gbp2 undergoes phase separation to form condensates that sequester SHP1. This sequestration facilitates STAT1 phosphorylation, which then downregulates SLC7A11, leading to ferroptosis and increased immunogenicity of dying cancer cells. Gbp2 overexpression is shown to increase T-cell infiltration, with this effect being attenuated in HMGB1 knockout models. Conversely, disruption of Gbp2 phase separation appears to promote tumor growth and reduce ICB efficacy.
While the authors have made a commendable effort to dissect the function and mechanism of Gbp2, several key issues remain unresolved. Most notably, it is unclear whether endogenous GBP2 condensates sequester SHP1 to a degree that facilitates STAT1 activation and ferroptosis, and whether GBP2 serves as a reliable biomarker for ICB response in patients.
Major Comments
1. There is an inconsistency between the basal levels of GBP2 in the “sgCtrl” group (Figure S5, panel a) versus the “Vec” group (panel b), despite consistent GAPDH loading controls and the expectation that these represent the same cell line. The authors should provide a clear explanation for the observed differences.
2. Data in Figures 2a and 2b indicate that GBP2 knockout cells display a growth advantage and reduced T-cell cytotoxicity regardless of ICB treatment, suggesting that GBP2 may act as a general mediator of T-cell cytotoxicity rather than being ICB-specific. The authors should provide additional data to support an ICB-specific role for GBP2 or adjust their claims to indicate that GBP2 functions as a general regulator of cell growth and T-cell toxicity.
3. In Figure 3a, the manuscript states that “A significant increase in SLC7A11 expression was found in GBP2-/- compared to sgCtrl cells, and this effect was restored by IFN-γ stimulation.” The authors need to provide quantitative analysis to support this claim and clarify what is meant by “restored”.
4. The in vitro co-culture experiments with ferrostatin-1 suggest that immune cell–derived factors may induce cancer cell death via ferroptosis. However, this does not establish ferroptosis as the predominant pathway underlying GBP2’s function in ICB. The authors should either present direct evidence that ferroptosis is the major mechanism (e.g., through rescue experiments with ferroptosis inhibitors or additional markers) or adjust their claims regarding the role of ferroptosis.
5. In Figure 5d, the manuscript indicates near-complete knockdown of GBP2 and SHP1 with siRNA, yet details regarding the siRNA sequences and a dose-response curve are missing. Please provide the siRNA sequences and include a dose-response analysis to validate knockdown efficiency.
6. In Figure 5e, it is unclear whether the data reflect endogenous GBP2 or transfected GBP2. Moreover, overexpression of GBP2 lacking its intrinsically disordered region fails to form condensates, does not sequester SHP1, and returns STAT1 phosphorylation to baseline, even though endogenous GBP2 should still be present. The authors should clarify these findings and explain the mechanism by which overexpression of a GBP2 variant without the IDR interferes with endogenous condensate formation.
7. The claim that SHP1 sequestration within GBP2 condensates blocks its function is not directly supported by the current data. Experiments demonstrating endogenous co-localization of GBP2 and SHP1 (e.g., via high-resolution imaging) are needed. Additionally, in vitro assays (such as reconstituted phosphorylation assays) showing that GBP2 condensates sequester SHP1 and impair STAT1 phosphorylation would strengthen this claim.
8. The authors could utilize two strategies to test the function of phase separation to strengthen their claims: (a) mutating specific amino acids to alter electrostatic and hydrophobic properties, and (b) fusing GBP2 to a hydrophilic sequence (e.g., MBP) to dampen self-association without altering the internal sequence.
9. In the first section, the manuscript claims that “bioinformatics analysis in clinical samples suggests that GBP2 is a potential combinatorial ICB treatment biomarker and is closely associated with CTL cytolytic activity.” As the analysis does not include direct ICB data, the conclusion that GBP2 is an ICB biomarker is not well-supported. The authors need to either incorporate ICB-specific data or rephrase the claim to reflect only the observed association with cytolytic activity.
10. It is unclear whether the clinical datasets analyzed in Figure 7 were obtained from patients before or after ICB treatment. The authors should specify the timing of these datasets to accurately interpret the correlation between GBP2 expression and ICB response.
Minor Comments:
1. The manuscript currently equates phase separation with biomolecular condensates by stating, “Phase separation, also known as biomolecular condensates…”.
However, phase separation is the process that gives rise to condensates; it is not synonymous with the condensate itself. The authors should revise this terminology to accurately reflect that phase separation underlies the formation of biomolecular condensates.
2. The manuscript lacks validation data for the Cas9 knockout experiments (e.g., confirming homozygous versus heterozygous knockout). Similarly, for the generation of mCherry-tagged GBP2 cells, it is unclear whether the knock-in is heterozygous or homozygous. Please provide genotyping data or additional validation to confirm the zygosity of these genetic modifications.
3. While immunostaining data are shown in Figure 2h, similar data for Figures 2f and 2g are lacking.
4. Some representative images are problematic. For instance, in Figure 2H, certain cells appear to be undergoing mitosis, and adjustments in image contrast (e.g., in Figure 5E) may lead to misinterpretation, such as displaying an abnormally large condensate that might be due to overexpression artifacts rather than physiological conditions.
5. The figure legend for Figure 6H is absent and should be provided.
6. For analyses based on published datasets, the manuscript should clearly indicate the origin of the data and include appropriate citations in the main text or figure legends.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The authors investigated the role of guanylate binding protein 2 (GBP2) in the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) and its underlying mechanisms in melanoma. They discovered that GBP2 can undergo phase separation through its intrinsically disordered region (IDR), which promotes STAT1 phosphorylation and inhibits SLC7A11 expression, ultimately leading to tumor ferroptosis. This work is conceptually intriguing, and the data largely support the authors' main claims. However, the quality of the manuscript could be enhanced by addressing the following points:
A. To better understand the immune-unrelated role of GBP2, it is recommended to test this in at least one in vivo model, such as an immune-deficient model.
B. While the mechanistic connection between GBP2, SHP1, and pSTAT1 has been thoroughly examined in vitro, it has not yet been evaluated in vivo. Given the novelty of this aspect, including in vivo studies is essential.
C. The data regarding HMGB1 and its participation in GBP-mediated tumor immunity are weak and somewhat tangential to the central message of the work. Omitting this section would sharpen the focus of the manuscript without compromising its significance.
D. The immunohistochemistry (IHC) data for SLC7A11 and GBP2 (Figures 3 and 7) should be re-evaluated concerning the specificity of antibodies, cell types, and localization.
E. The discussion could benefit from including the selectivity and involvement of other GBP family members in ICB.
By addressing these points, the authors could significantly enhance the clarity and impact of their findings.
