peer_review_rounds.author_response:
RESPONSES TO REVIEWERS
We would like to express our sincere thanks to all three reviewers for their critical and
constructive comments. We have performed substantial additional experiments to
address their concerns. We respond point-by-point to each of their comments and
criticisms. We feel that their comments have helped us on significantly improving and
strengthening the manuscript and clarifying some issues. We hope that the revision
has addressed their major concerns.
Reviewer #1
This manuscript explores the role of GBP2 in immunogenic ferroptosis and ICB
response in tumors, an intriguing and relevant topic in cancer immunotherapy. The
authors provide a detailed analysis integrating bioinformatics, in vivo models, and
molecular analyses to establish a link between GBP2, phase separation, and STAT1
activation in the tumor microenvironment. However, in some cases, the conclusions
are based solely on correlations and require further validation to fully support the
proposed model.
1. CRISPR/Cas9 Off-Target Effects: The use of CRISPR/Cas9 technology can lead to
off-target mutations. How did the authors verify that the generated cell lines do not
carry unintended genetic alterations? A proper validation should be included to ensure
the accuracy of the reported data.
Response:
Following the reviewer’s advice, we conducted a series of experiments to rigorously
assess potential off-target effects associated with gene editing. First, sgRNAs were
designed using Benchling platform to maximize on-target efficiency while minimizing
off-target effects. To validate the robustness and reproducibility of our findings, we
replicated key experiments both in vitro and in vivo across three independent tumor
models: B16-OVA, MC38-OVA, and A375. This approach helped to exclude the
possibility of cell line–specific artifacts.
Furthermore, to rule out potential off-target effects of CRISPR/Cas9 editing, we
adopted a rescue strategy based on the approach described by Manguso et al. (Nature.
OVA cells. As expected, overexpression of GBP2 (oeGBP2) significantly restored the
expression of SLC7A11 and the phosphorylation of STAT1 (Fig. S7K). More
importantly, enforced GBP2 expression also restored lipid ROS accumulation and
reinstated GBP2-/- tumor cells to anti-PD-L1 therapy in vivo (Fig. S7L-M). These
findings strongly suggest that the enhanced ferroptotic sensitivity and
immunotherapeutic response observed in GBP2-deficient models are not attributable
to off-target effects.
According to the reviewer’s suggestion, we added the new data in the revised
manuscript, page 22 line 489-493 and Fig. S7K-M.
Part new figures are shown below.
Fig. S7: (K) The GBP2-/- B16-OVA cells transfected with GBP2 plasmid (oe-GBP2), then
treated with 10 ng/mL IFN-γ for 12 hours, and cell lysates were collected and analyzed by
western blot. (L) The GBP2-/- and GBP2-/- + oeGBP2 B16-OVA (1 × 106) cells subcutaneously
injected into C57BL/6 mice. Mice with a tumor size of 125 mm3 were treated with anti–PD-L1
antibody or IgG once per 3 days. (M) Relative lipid ROS of Ctrl, GBP2-/- and GBP2-/- + GBP2oe
tumours in mice treated with anti-PD-L1 were quantified in CD45- cells by flow cytometric
analysis.
2. IFN-γ and Ferroptosis: The authors suggest that IFN-γ induces ferroptosis via GBP2;
however, this is not supported by experimental data. To clarify this, cytokine levels
should be measured in tumours derived from GBP2-/- and control cells (with or without
ICB) to assess IFN-γ and other relevant cytokines in the tumour microenvironment.
This would also help determine the inflammatory status in the presence or absence of
GBP2 in the context of ICB. Additionally, in vivo IFN-γ blocking experiments should be
performed to establish a functional link between GBP2 and IFN-γ.
Response:
We acknowledge the reviewer's insightful comment. It will be critical to elucidate the
precise molecular and cellular mechanisms by which the immune system regulates
ferroptotic cell death. The seminal study by Wang et al. first demonstrated that
immunotherapy-activated CD8⁺ T cells enhance tumor cell-specific lipid peroxidation
through released IFN-γ, thereby augmenting anti-tumor efficacy (Nature. 2019
May;569(7755):270-274). Recent studies have further elucidated potential
mechanisms of IFN-γ-induced tumor ferroptosis (Nat Chem Biol. 2025 Apr 25. doi:
10.1038/s41589-025-01887-3; Cancer Cell. 2022 Apr 11;40(4):365-378.e6; Cell Mol
Life Sci. 2022 Jun 8;79(7):352; J Immunother Cancer. 2022 Jun;10(6):e004381). Our
study aims to identify GBP2 as one potential mediator in IFN-γ-driven ferroptosis.
However, it should be noted that we currently lack experimental data explicitly
demonstrating that IFN-γ induces ferroptosis specifically through GBP2.
To clarify this, we first performed ELISA to assess cytokine levels (primarily
IFN-γ and TNF-α) in sgCtrl and sgGBP2 tumors with or without anti-PD-L1 treatment.
These cytokines are critically involved in CD8+T cell-mediated killing during immune
checkpoint blockade (ICB) (Nature. 2025 Apr;640(8060):1062-1071). Under baseline
conditions (no anti-PD-L1), GBP2 deficiency did not alter IFN-γ or TNF-α levels versus
controls. During early-phase anti-PD-L1 treatment (Day 7), we observed modest yet
significant increases in IFN-γ and TNF-α relative to IgG-treated tumors. However,
GBP2 knockout did not significantly attenuate this cytokine elevation. Strikingly, in
late-phase treatment (Day 14), anti-PD-L1 induced substantially heightened release
of these cytokines (tumor weight-normalized) versus IgG controls (Fig. 2K and Fig.
S6H). And this effect was potently suppressed by GBP2 depletion (Fig. 2K and Fig.
S6H). We interpret this temporal divergence as potentially attributable to GBP2-
dependent immunogenic ferroptosis in later stages. Specifically, GBP2 activation may
trigger DAMPs release from ferroptotic cells, subsequently recruiting dendritic cells
and amplifying CD8+ T cell activation, thereby initiating a positive feedback loop that
augments anti-tumor immunity.
To further identify the specific cytokine mediating this effect, we generated
perforin-/-, IFNγ-/-, or TNFα-/- OT-1 cells and co-cultured them with control versus
GBP2-overexpressing B16-OVA tumor cells. Critically, loss of IFN-γ, but not perforin
or TNF-α, prevented OT-1-cell-mediated killing of GBP2-overexpressing tumors (Fig.
2L). Furthermore, we performed blocking experiments as suggested by the reviewer.
We found that GBP2 overexpression enhanced both ICB efficacy and lipid ROS
production (Fig. 2M and Fig. S6I). These effects were abrogated by anti-IFN-γ
monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) (Fig. 2M and Fig. S6I). Collectively, these data
demonstrate that GBP2 mechanistically facilitates IFN-γ-dependent tumor ferroptosis,
thereby potentiating ICB therapeutic efficacy.
According to the reviewer’s suggestion, we added the new data in the revised
manuscript, page19-20 line 421-439 and Fig. 2K-M and Fig. S6H-I.
Part new figures are shown below.
Fig. 2: (K) The protein levels of IFN-γ in tumor lysates were quantified by ELISA in mice
treated with anti–PD-L1 antibody or control IgG. (L) Viability of vector (Vec) or GBP2-
overexpressing (GBP2oe) B16-OVA tumor cells after 24-hours co-culture with OT-1 T cells
transduced with sgCtrl, sgIFNγ, sgTNFα, or sgPRF1 at an effector-to-target (E:T) ratio of 1:1
(n = 3 per group). (M) Vec or GBP2oe B16-OVA cells (1 × 10⁶) were subcutaneously implanted
into C57BL/6 mice. When tumors reached ~125 mm³, mice were treated with anti-PD-L1, anti-
IFN-γ, or control IgG antibodies every 3 days.
Fig. S6: (H) The protein levels of TNF-α in tumor lysates were quantified by ELISA in mice
treated with anti–PD-L1 antibody or control IgG. (I) Relative lipid ROS of B16-OVA tumors in
mice treated with anti-IFN-γ were quantified in CD45- cells by flow cytometric analysis.
3. FRAP Analysis: The FRAP data presented are incomplete. To fully characterize
GBP2 phase separation properties, appropriate controls should be included, such as
a protein known to form condensates and a protein known to remain solubilized. This
comparison would help determine whether GBP2 phase separation follows a typical
liquid-liquid phase separation behaviour.
Response:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. To rigorously evaluate
the biophysical properties of GBP2 condensates, we have incorporated both positive
and negative controls, as recommended. Following established protocols from Liu et
al. (Cell, 2021, 184(22):5559–5576) and Cai et al. (Nat Cell Biol, 2019, 21(12):1578–
1589), we used glycogen as a positive control and mCherry alone as a negative control
in our fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) experiments. Under
identical conditions, glycogen condensates displayed rapid fluorescence recovery
after photobleaching, consistent with liquid-like dynamics. In contrast, mCherry
exhibited minimal recovery, validating its role as a non-phase-separating control.
These results confirm the robustness of our FRAP assay and demonstrate that GBP2
condensates possess dynamic fluidity—characteristic of biologically functional,
phase-separated structures.
In accordance with the reviewer’s suggestion, we have incorporated these new data
into the revised manuscript (page 23 line 509-514; Fig. S8D-E.)
Part new figures are shown below.
Fig. S8: (D) Representative images showed that FRAP assay of the droplets of glycogen
formed in B16-OVA cells. The data are plotted as the mean ± SD on the right (n = 3). (E)
Representative images showed that FRAP assay of the droplets formed in B16-OVA cells
expressing mCherry. The data are plotted as the mean ± SD on the right (n = 3).
4. GBP2ΔIDR and ICB Response: The authors demonstrate that GBP2ΔIDR reduces
CD8+ OT-1 cytotoxicity; however, they do not assess whether GBP2 phase separation
is required for ICB efficacy in vivo. A murine model with GBP2ΔIDR + anti-PD-L1
should be used to determine if GBP2 condensation is necessary for a successful ICB
response.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this critical point and acknowledge our oversight in
addressing GBP2 phase separation in vivo. To determine whether GBP2 phase
separation is essential for ICB efficacy, we established tumor-bearing mouse models
with GBP2ΔIDR + anti-PD-L1 treatment as suggested. As suggested, the results
showed that under anti–PD-L1 treatment, tumors expressing GBP2-ΔIDR exhibited a
marked reduction in therapeutic response compared to the GBP2-FL group, as well
as diminished ROS production (Fig. 5K-L). Furthermore, it was reported that in vivo
phase separation could observe aggregation foci under immunofluorescence (Cell.
the aforementioned tumor specimens to visualize this phenomenon. Critically, distinct
GBP2 aggregate foci were readily detectable in GBP2-FL tumors following anti-PD-L1
treatment, whereas such structures were absent in GBP2-ΔIDR tumors (Fig. 5N).
According to the reviewer’s suggestion, we added the new data in the revised
manuscript (page 26 line 564-565,568-572; Fig. 5K-L, N).
Part new figures are shown below.
Fig. 5: (K) 1 × 106 GBP2-/- B16-OVA cells expressing GBP2-FL and GBP2 △IDR were
subcutaneously injected into C57BL/6 mice. (left) Mice with a tumor size of 125 mm3 were
treated with anti–PD-L1 antibody or IgG once per 3 days. FL, full length. (right) Tumor
inhibition rate for GBP2 △IDR under anti-PD-L1 treatment, respectively (n = 6). (L) Relative
lipid ROS of GBP2-FL or GBP2 △IDR tumours in mice treated with anti-PD-L1 were quantified
in CD45− cells by flow cytometric analysis. (N) Representative images of GBP2 of
immunofluorescent staining in GBP2-FL or GBP2 △IDR tumours under anti-PD-L1 treatment
(n = 3).
5. Immune Infiltration Profiling: The authors suggest that GBP2 may modulate immune
responses by promoting immunogenic cell death. Since this mechanism has
significant implications for immune cells, a more comprehensive analysis of tumour-
infiltrating leukocytes should be performed. This should not be limited to CD8+ T cells
and DCs but should include a full leukocyte profile in mice transplanted with GBP2-/-
and sgGBP2 tumour cells, with or without or with ICB therapy. Additionally, the authors should
assess whether CD8+ T cells show increased activation in sgGBP2 tumours.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this critical point. Following the reviewer's suggestion,
performed flow cytometric profiling of tumor-infiltrating leukocytes in anti‑PD‑L1–
treated sgGBP2 and sgCtrl tumors. Utilizing the gating strategy established by Guo et
al. (Nature. 2023 Aug;620(7972):200-208), we quantified the major immune subsets,
including CD8⁺ T cells, CD4⁺ T cells, NK cells, B cells, neutrophils,
monocytes/macrophages, and dendritic cells (Fig. S10B). The results showed that
anti-PD-L1 treatment significantly increased the proportions of CD8⁺ T cells, CD4⁺ T
cells, NK cells and B cells. Critically, regardless of PD-L1 treatment, GBP2 deletion
substantially suppressed infiltration of CD8⁺ T cells, while exerting no significant effect
on CD4⁺ T cells, dendritic cells, B cells, NK cells, monocytes/macrophages, or
neutrophils (Fig. 6A). These results demonstrate that GBP2 shapes an
immunostimulatory tumor microenvironment (TME) through regulating CD8+T cell
infiltration.
Furthermore, we quantified the activation status of CD8⁺ T cells by assessing the
proportions of IFN-γ⁺ and TNF-α⁺ T cell subsets (Nat Commun. 2020 Sep
24;11(1):4835). Flow cytometric analysis of CD8⁺ T cell activation markers showed
that GBP2 ablation markedly attenuated IFN-γ⁺ and TNF-α⁺ CD8⁺ T cell frequencies
(Fig. 6E). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that GBP2 potentiates CD8+T cell-
mediated anti-tumor immunity.
According to the reviewer’s suggestion, we added the new data in the revised
manuscript (page 26-27 line 583-589,592-595; and Fig. 6A, E and Fig. S10B).
Part new figures are shown below.
Fig. S10B: Gating strategies for flow cytometry analysis and cell sorting.
Fig. 6A: Percentage of tumor infiltrating immune subsets between sgCtrl and GBP2-/- tumours
with or without anti-PD-L1 in B16-OVA-bearing mice. n = 3 mice.
Fig. 6E: Representative images and statistical quantitation of the flow cytometric analysis of
the percentage of IFN-γ+CD8+ and TNF-α+CD8+ TILs from sgCtrl and sgGBP2 xenografts.
6. Manuscript Readability and Clarity: The manuscript should be carefully revised to
improve clarity and readability. Lines 273-275 contain a sentence that appears
incorrect and contradicts the data presented. Please revise this section for accuracy.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the ambiguity in Lines 273–275. The sentence
in question has been revised to eliminate any confusion and to ensure full consistency
with the data presented. In addition, we have conducted a comprehensive language
revision throughout the manuscript to improve clarity, precision, and overall readability.
All changes have been highlighted in the revised version.
Reviewer #2
Summary:
Liu et al performed a weighted network correlation analysis of immune checkpoint
blockade-treated patients and identified GBP2 as a potential driver of ICB response.
They find that loss of GBP2 ablates PD-L1 response in mouse models and argue that
GBP2 acts to enhance T-cell-mediated ferroptosis via modulation of SLCA11 in an
IFN-dependent manner. They further argue that GBP2 forms phase-separated
condensates that sequester SHP1 and thereby promote STAT1 phosphorylation and
subsequent induction of SLCA11. They seek to validate this finding in patient cohorts
and argue that GBP2 acts to support ferroptosis, immunogenicity cell death and
HMGB1 expression.
Overall the group presents a large body of intriguing data. The finding that GBP2
modulates and supports IFNg / STAT1 signaling via phase separated sequestration of
SHP1 is interesting. They separately show that GBP2 loss impairs ferroptosis and that
this impairment can be overcome by SLCA11 knockdown. Each of these findings
represents a meaningful contribution to the field and, in particular, the work supporting
SHP1 sequestration by GBP2 seems to me to be a strength. That said, there are also
some concerns with the paper as currently constructed.
Major Concerns:
There are some logical leaps that I worry are not fully justified by the data. For example,
because loss of GBP2 affects STAT1 signaling and STAT signaling affects many
pathways of immunotherapy response (not least, MHC-I expression, expression of
checkpoint ligands, CD8+ T cell and NK cell recognition), I am not sure that the data
connecting GBP2 with ferroptosis and the data connecting GBP2 with immunotherapy
response are necessarily connected. The authors could strengthen this connection by
testing whether SLCA11 overexpression in tumor cells ablates the in vivo GBP2 PD-
L1 response phenotype they observe. I would also recommend evaluating alternative
or complementary hypotheses by testing the expression of other IFN-stimulated genes
such as MHC-I in GBP2 ko cell lines. Finally, the authors rely heavily on a single
mouse model for in vivo studies and could benefit from repeating core findings (e.g.
GBP2 sensitization to PD-L1) in an additional model to support its robustness.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this critical and insightful point. We fully agree that
STAT1 plays a pivotal role in tumor immunology, including the regulation of MHC-I
expression, immune checkpoint ligands, and immune cell recognition (Signal
Transduct Target Ther. 2021, 6:402). In response, we performed a series of
experiments to evaluate these alternative or complementary mechanisms, as
suggested.
To address the reviewer’s concern regarding MHC-I expression, we wish to clarify
that our B16-OVA and MC38-OVA tumor models were engineered using the
PresentER system (Elife. 2018 Nov 30;7:e41090), which enables stable expression of
peptide/MHC-I complexes. As a result, these cells constitutively overexpress both
OVA antigen and MHC-I molecules, eliminating the possibility that reduced
immunotherapy efficacy in the GBP2-knockout context is due to altered MHC-I
presentation. This was further confirmed by flow cytometric analysis, which revealed
no significant differences in surface MHC-I expression between sgCtrl and sgGBP2
tumor cells (Fig. S7E-F).
We next examined checkpoint ligand expression. Western blot analysis showed
that GBP2 knockout did not alter PD-L1 levels in tumor cells, either at baseline or
following IFN-γ stimulation (Fig. S7G). To assess CD8⁺ T and NK cell interactions with
tumor cells, we employed the FucoID platform (Cell. 2020 Nov 12;183(4):1117–1133),
a technique that quantifies cell-cell interactions based on fucosyl-biotinylation. FucoID
analysis revealed no significant differences in immune cell–tumor cell interaction
frequencies between sgCtrl and sgGBP2 groups (Fig. S7H).
Taken together, these results suggest that the impact of GBP2 on antitumor
immunity is unlikely to be mediated through canonical STAT1-driven pathways such
as MHC-I or PD-L1 expression or changes in immune cell–tumor cell interactions.
Instead, our data support the hypothesis that GBP2 regulates tumor ferroptosis
through the STAT1/SLC7A11 axis.
In our initial submission, we demonstrated that silencing SLC7A11 via siRNA in
GBP2-deficient B16-OVA cells restored lipid ROS accumulation following RSL3
treatment under IFN-γ priming (Fig. 3C). Moreover, GBP2 knockout significantly
elevated intracellular GSH levels and increased cell viability—effects that were
reversed by SLC7A11 silencing (Fig. 3D). In line with the reviewer’s suggestion, we
have now performed complementary in vivo experiments. Overexpression of
SLC7A11 in tumor cells significantly diminished the tumor-suppressive effect of GBP2
overexpression, reduced intratumoral lipid ROS levels, and abolished GBP2-mediated
enhancement of ICB efficacy (Fig. 3E-F).
Lastly, to validate the robustness and generalizability of our findings, we extended
our analysis to an independent tumor model using the MC38-OVA colon carcinoma
line (Nature. 2025 Apr;640(8060):1062–1071; Nat Commun. 2022 Sep 6;13(1):4981).
GBP2 knockout in MC38-OVA cells was confirmed by western blotting (Fig. S5D).
In both OT-1 adoptive transfer and anti-PD-L1 treatment settings, GBP2 deficiency
significantly impaired therapeutic responses (Fig. S5E-H), recapitulating our findings
in the B16-OVA model.
In accordance with the reviewer’s suggestion, we have included these new data
in the revised manuscript (page 21 line 457-460; page 18-19, line 402-404; page 22,
line 467-481; and Fig. 3E-F and Fig. S5D-H and Fig. S7E-H).
Part new figures are shown below.
Fig. S7: (E-F) Representative flow cytometry plots and quantification showing H-2Kb bound
to SIINFEKL in sgCtrl and GBP2-/- B16-OVA and MC38-OVA groups. (G) The sgCtrl and
GBP2-/- B16-OVA and A375 cells were treated with 10 ng/mL IFN-γ for 12 hours, respectively.
Cell lysates were collected and analyzed the indicated molecules by western blot. (H)The
sgCtrl and GBP2-/- B16-OVA cells co-cultured with CD8+T or NK cells were co-incubated in
the presence of biotin–LPETG for 30 min and analyzed by flow cytometry. The extent of
labelling of tumor cells between groups.
Fig. 3: (E) 1 × 106 vector, GBP2-overexpression (oeGBP2) and oeGBP2 transfected with
oeSLC7A11 plasmid B16-OVA cells were subcutaneously injected into C57BL/6 mice. All
mice with a tumor size of 125 mm3 were treated with anti-PD-L1 antibody or IgG once per 3
days. (F) Relative lipid ROS of vector, oeGBP2 or oeGBP2 + oeSLC7A11 tumours in mice
treated with anti-PD-L1 were quantified in CD45− cells by flow cytometric analysis.
Fig. S5: (D) Western blot showed the transfection efficiency of sgGBP2 in MC38-OVA cells.
(E) The sgCtrl or GBP2-/- MC38-OVA (1 × 106) cells subcutaneously injected into C57BL/6
mice. Mice were adoptively transferred with OT-1 cells (5 × 106 per mouse) or PBS once per
7 days. (F) Tumor inhibition rate for GBP2-/- cells relative to sgCtrl cells under OT-1 treatment,
respectively (n = 6). (G) The sgCtrl or GBP2-/- MC38-OVA (1 × 106) cells subcutaneously
injected into C57BL/6 mice. Mice with a tumor size of 125 mm3 were treated with anti–PD-L1
antibody (200 μg per mouse) or IgG once per 3 days. (H) Tumor inhibition rate for GBP2-/-
cells relative to sgCtrl cells under anti-PD-L1 treatment, respectively (n = 6).
I am additionally concerned about the potential for circular reasoning in the patient
correlative studies: better clinical responses with GBP2, more immunogenic tumor cell
death or more CD8+ T cells may not be all that surprising given that GBP2 is an ISG.
Indeed, correlations are presented between IFN-signatures (composed of ISGs) and
GBP2. In this case it seems quite possible that cause and effect may be reversed–
that GBP2 expression is the effect of ISG induction rather than the cause, as is claimed.
By comparison, analysis could equally be conducted simply asking if IFN signaling in
tumors correlates with CD8+ T cell infiltration or whether they respond better to
immunotherapy–both well established observations in the field.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this expert commentary. It is well established that tumor cell
responsiveness to IFN-γ is a critical determinant of both ICB efficacy and anti-tumor
immunity (Nat Rev Cancer. 2022 Apr;22(4):195-207). CRISPR-Cas9 screens have
repeatedly identified IFN-γ signaling components among the top genes associated
with ICB responsiveness (Nature. 2017 Aug 31;548(7669):537-542; Science. 2018
Feb 16;359(6377):770-775). Many interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) are not merely
markers but functional mediators of anti-tumor effects. For example, the lncRNA LIMIT
activates the GBP gene cluster to potentiate tumor immunogenicity and ICB efficacy
(Nat Cell Biol. 2021 May;23(5):526-537), and ACSL4 links IFN-γ to ferroptosis
induction, improving ICB outcomes (Cancer Cell. 2022 Apr 11;40(4):365-378.e6).
These findings illustrate that ISGs can actively amplify IFN-γ-driven anti-tumor
immunity, suggesting that GBP2 might similarly function as an effector rather than a
passive biomarker.
Our current results indicate that sgGBP2 attenuates ICB efficacy primarily by
reducing ICB-mediated ferroptosis. Mechanistically, as suggested by the reviewer, we
found that GBP2 primarily activates the STAT1 signaling pathway to influence
ferroptosis independently of STAT1-related MHC-I expression, immune checkpoint
expression, and CD8+ T/NK cell recognition. Regarding the concern about MHC-I
expression, we wish to clarify that we utilized the PresentER system (Elife. 2018 Nov
30:7:e41090), which enables the encoding of multiple peptide/MHC complexes. Thus,
our B16-OVA and MC38-OVA model constitutively overexpressed both OVA and
MHC-I components and the scenario of concern to the reviewer does not exist.
Furthermore, we performed flow cytometry analysis of MHC-I expression and
observed no significant changes between the sgCtrl and sgGBP2 group (Fig. S7E-F).
Additionally, we assessed the expression of checkpoint ligands, focusing on PD-L1.
Western blot analysis of sgGBP2 cells revealed no significant difference in PD-L1
expression levels compared to sgCtrl—both with and without IFN-γ stimulation (Fig.
S7G). We also employed FucoID technology (Cell. 2020 Nov 12; 183(4): 1117–1133).
In brief, FucoID can evaluate cell-to-cell interactions based on an interaction dependent
fucosyl-biotinylation. As a result, no significant differences were observed between
sgCtrl and sgGBP2 group (Fig. S7H).
We attribute these results to significantly diminished IFN-γ signaling upon GBP2
knockout, which consequently elevates SLC7A11 expression to inhibit ferroptosis.
This suppression results in reduced DAMPs release, impaired dendritic cell
recruitment, and subsequently diminished CD8⁺ T cell activation, culminating in
compromised anti-tumor immunity. However, we acknowledge that our existing data
lack definitive experimental validation to establish a direct causal relationship between
GBP2 and IFN-γ signaling.
Therefore, we first performed ELISA to assess cytokine levels (primarily IFN-γ
and TNF-α) in sgCtrl and sgGBP2 tumors with or without anti-PD-L1 treatment. These
cytokines are critically involved in CD8+T cell-mediated killing during immune
checkpoint blockade (ICB) (Nature. 2025 Apr;640(8060):1062-1071). Under baseline
conditions (no anti-PD-L1), GBP2 deficiency did not alter IFN-γ or TNF-α levels versus
controls. During early-phase anti-PD-L1 treatment (Day 7), we observed modest yet
significant increases in IFN-γ and TNF-αrelative to IgG-treated tumors. However,
GBP2 knockout did not significantly attenuate this cytokine elevation. Strikingly, in
late-phase treatment (Day 14), anti-PD-L1 induced substantially heightened release
of these cytokines (tumor weight-normalized) versus IgG controls (Fig. 2K and Fig.
S6H). And this effect was potently suppressed by GBP2 depletion (Fig. 2K and Fig.
S6H). We interpret this temporal divergence as potentially attributable to GBP2-
dependent immunogenic ferroptosis in later stages. Specifically, GBP2 activation may
trigger DAMPs release from ferroptotic cells, subsequently recruiting dendritic cells
and amplifying CD8+ T cell activation, thereby initiating a positive feedback loop that
augments anti-tumor immunity.
To further identify the specific cytokine mediating this effect, we generated
perforin-/-, IFNγ-/-, or TNFα-/- OT-1 cells and co-cultured them with control versus
GBP2-overexpressing B16-OVA tumor cells. Critically, loss of IFN-γ, but not perforin
or TNF, prevented OT-1-cell-mediated killing of GBP2-overexpressing tumors (Fig.
2L). Furthermore, we performed blocking experiments as suggested by the reviewer.
We found that GBP2 overexpression enhanced both ICB efficacy and lipid ROS
production (Fig. 2M and Fig. S6I). These effects were abrogated by anti-IFN-γ
monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) (Fig. 2M and Fig. S6I). To mitigate confounding effects
from CD8+T cell infiltration, we intratumorally injected equal numbers of OT-1 cells.
Under these standardized conditions, we observed comparable levels of secreted IFN-
γ across experimental groups. However, sgGBP2 tumors exhibited significantly
reduced lipid ROS accumulation and accelerated tumor growth relative to controls
(Figure for reviewer). Furthermore, rescue experiments demonstrated that GBP2
restoration (GBP2-/- + oeGBP2) reversed this phenotype, yielding smaller tumors with
elevated lipid ROS levels (Fig. S7K-M). Collectively, these data establish that GBP2
sensitizes tumor cell to IFN-γ-mediated ferroptosis, thereby potentiating ICB
therapeutic efficacy.
Additionally, we acknowledge that our study does not explore the upstream
regulatory mechanisms controlling GBP2 expression, which may contribute to the
observed heterogeneity of GBP2 levels in patient tumor samples. Epigenetic
regulation is a well-recognized mechanism of gene silencing (Nat Immunol. 2024
Oct;25(10):1858–1870; Sci Transl Med. 2023 Feb;15(681):eabq6024) and has
recently emerged as a conserved means of regulating GBP family gene expression in
cancer. For instance, GBP4 promoter hypomethylation has been reported in
pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma relative to adjacent normal tissue, and targeted
promoter methylation suppresses GBP4 expression (Cancer Immunol Immunother.
prognosis in gastric cancer (Clin Epigenetics. 2020 Jan 20;12(1):15), and GBP2
methylation levels in plasma correlate with advanced stages of breast cancer (Genet
Mol Biol. 2020 Nov 17;43(4):e20190230). In line with these findings, we observed a
significant inverse correlation between GBP2 expression and DNA methylation levels
in melanoma (Figure for reviewer), further supporting the hypothesis that DNA
methylation may drive GBP2 silencing in tumors. While this epigenetic regulation
represents a compelling area for further research, our current study is specifically
focused on elucidating the functional role of GBP2 in modulating response to immune
checkpoint blockade. Detailed mechanistic investigation into the epigenetic regulation
of GBP2 is ongoing and will be addressed in future studies. Accordingly, we have
included this discussion in the revised manuscript's Discussion section.

- Is GBP2 genetically lost / selected against in tumors? The authors’ findings would
predict that it should be, given that this is claimed to induce resistance to anti-tumor
immunity in an immunogenic disease.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for raising this critical point. The genetic status of tumors is
indeed a major determinant of response to ICB therapy (Cell. 2021 Oct
14;184(21):5309–5337). Accordingly, it is essential to investigate whether GBP2 is
genetically lost or selectively downregulated in tumors.
First, integrative analyses using spatial transcriptomics (Fig. 1I) and newly
acquired clinical melanoma specimens (Figure for reviewer. A) consistently revealed
reduced GBP2 expression in melanoma tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues.
To explore potential genetic mechanisms underlying this downregulation, we analyzed
somatic mutation rates in melanoma using data from The Cancer Genome Atlas
(TCGA). A waterfall plot illustrating the top 20 most frequently mutated genes, along
with GBP2, showed that the somatic mutation rate of GBP2 is very low (~2%) (Figure
for reviewer. B), suggesting that genetic mutation is unlikely to be the major
mechanism underlying GBP2 loss.
Beyond genetic alterations, epigenetic regulation represents a well-established
alternative mechanism for gene silencing (Nat Immunol. 2024 Oct;25(10):1858–1870;
Sci Transl Med. 2023 Feb;15(681):eabq6024). Recent studies have demonstrated that
epigenetic dysregulation is a conserved mechanism modulating GBP family gene
expression across various cancers. For instance, GBP4 promoter hypomethylation
has been observed in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma relative to adjacent normal
tissue, and targeted promoter methylation suppresses GBP4 expression (Cancer
Immunol Immunother. 2024 Aug 7;73(10):208). Similarly, GBP6 hypermethylation
predicts poor prognosis in gastric cancer (Clin Epigenetics. 2020 Jan 20;12(1):15),
while plasma GBP2 methylation levels correlate with advanced stages of breast
cancer (Genet Mol Biol. 2020 Nov 17;43(4):e20190230). Consistent with these
findings, we observed a strong negative correlation between GBP2 expression and
DNA methylation in melanoma samples (Figure for reviewer. C). These results
collectively suggest that DNA methylation-mediated silencing may represent a
plausible mechanism for GBP2 downregulation in tumors. While this epigenetic axis
is of significant interest, our current study focuses primarily on the functional and
mechanistic role of GBP2 in modulating ICB responses. Investigation of upstream
epigenetic regulation remains an important component of our ongoing work and is
therefore discussed in the revised manuscript's Discussion and Limitations sections
Second, regarding the question of whether GBP2 is under negative selective
pressure in tumors: the concept of "selected against" implies that tumor cells lose
GBP2 expression to gain a survival advantage. To address this, we analyzed publicly
available screening data and found that GBP2 expression was positively correlated
with OT-1-mediated cytotoxicity (Figure for reviewer. D), akin to known components
of the IFN-γ signaling pathway such as STAT1, B2M, and TAP1. This supports a role
for GBP2 in promoting anti-tumor immune responses. These findings suggest that
tumors may actively suppress GBP2 expression as an immune evasion strategy.
Consistently, GBP2 knockout rendered tumor cells resistant to immune-mediated
killing.
In response to reviewers' comments and considering space constraints and
overall manuscript flow, the relevant results are presented in the corresponding figure
panels below (Figure for reviewer. A-D). Given that the primary aim of this study is to
elucidate the mechanisms by which GBP2 enhances ICB efficacy, we have discussed
these insights in the revised Discussion and Limitations section. Future studies are
warranted to further dissect the upstream regulatory mechanisms governing GBP2
expression.

Reviewer #3
The manuscript titled “Gbp2 condensate promote ferroptosis, sensitize anti-PD-L1 ICB
in melanoma” investigates the role of Gbp2 in enhancing immune checkpoint blockade
(ICB) in a mouse model. The authors propose that under IFN-γ stimulation, Gbp2
undergoes phase separation to form condensates that sequester SHP1. This
sequestration facilitates STAT1 phosphorylation, which then downregulates SLC7A11,
leading to ferroptosis and increased immunogenicity of dying cancer cells. Gbp2
overexpression is shown to increase T-cell infiltration, with this effect being attenuated

appears to promote tumor growth and reduce ICB efficacy.

mechanism of Gbp2, several key issues remain unresolved. Most notably, it is unclear
whether endogenous GBP2 condensates sequester SHP1 to a degree that facilitates
STAT1 activation and ferroptosis, and whether GBP2 serves as a reliable biomarker
for ICB response in patients.

2. Data in Figures 2a and 2b indicate that GBP2 knockout cells display a growth
advantage and reduced T-cell cytotoxicity regardless of ICB treatment, suggesting that
GBP2 may act as a general mediator of T-cell cytotoxicity rather than being ICB-

Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. In the tumor microenvironment,
excessive activation of immune checkpoint pathways suppresses T cell cytotoxicity,
facilitating immune evasion. The therapeutic efficacy of ICB is primarily attributed to
the reinvigoration of tumor-specific CD8⁺ T cells (Cell. 2021 Oct 14;184(21):5309-5337;
Science. 2018 Mar 23;359(6382):1350-1355). These reinvigorated T cells recognize
MHC-I–peptide complexes on tumor cells via their specific TCRs, triggering the
release of cytolytic granules and IFN-γ, which mediate tumor cell killing (Nature. 2023
Jun;618(7967):1033-1040).
Despite its clinical benefits, ICB is effective in only a subset of patients, prompting
intensive efforts to identify novel targets that enhance CTL-mediated killing and
potentiate ICB efficacy. For example, VDAC2 has been reported as an
immunoregulatory checkpoint that attenuates T cell–derived IFN-γ–mediated tumor
destruction and suppresses inflammatory reprogramming of the tumor
microenvironment. Inhibiting VDAC2 sensitizes tumor cells to IFN-γ–induced cell
death, thereby significantly enhancing antitumor immunity and ICB responsiveness
(Nature. 2025 Apr;640(8060):1062-1071). Similarly, Liao et al. demonstrated that
CTL-derived IFN-γ and tumor microenvironmental arachidonic acid synergistically
induce ACSL4-dependent ferroptosis, and targeting ACSL4 increases tumor
susceptibility to ICB therapy (Cancer Cell. 2022 Apr 11;40(4):365-378.e6).
In this study, bioinformatic screening identified GBP2 as a key regulator positively
correlated with T cell cytotoxicity. We performed comprehensive in vivo and in vitro
analyses to validate GBP2’s impact on T cell–mediated tumor elimination. First,
sgGBP2 tumors implanted in immunodeficient NSG mice exhibited comparable growth
between sgCtrl and sgGBP2 groups (Fig. S5C), indicating that GBP2 primarily
mediates tumor suppression through immune regulation. Given the pivotal role of
CD8⁺ T cells in antitumor immunity, we next depleted CD8⁺ T cells and found that
tumor growth in the oeGBP2 group was markedly increased (Fig. 6D), underscoring
the CD8⁺ T cell dependency of GBP2-mediated effects.
To assess whether GBP2 specifically influences ICB-mediated killing, we
compared PD-L1 expression after sgGBP2 knockout and observed no significant
changes (Fig. S7G). To eliminate potential confounding from MHC-I modulation, we
engineered B16-OVA cells (following Gejman et al., Elife. 2018 Nov 30;7:e41090) to
constitutively express both OVA and MHC-I components. Flow cytometry confirmed
no significant differences in MHC-I levels between sgCtrl and sgGBP2 cells (Fig. S7E-
F).
CD8⁺ T cells activated by cancer immunotherapy primarily clear tumors via
perforin–granzyme and Fas–FasL pathways (Nat Rev Immunol. 2018 Aug;18(8):527-
535). To identify the specific effector molecule involved, we generated perforin⁻/⁻,
IFNγ⁻/⁻, or TNFα⁻/⁻ OT-1 cells and co-cultured them with control or GBP2-
overexpressing B16-OVA tumor cells. Loss of IFN-γ, but not perforin or TNF, 
abrogated OT-1–mediated killing of GBP2-overexpressing tumors (Fig. 2L).
Furthermore, as suggested by the reviewer, we performed blocking experiments,
showing that GBP2 overexpression enhanced both ICB efficacy and lipid ROS
accumulation (Fig. 2M and Fig. S6I), effects that were completely abolished by anti–
IFN-γ monoclonal antibodies (Fig. 2M and Fig. S6I). Consistent with Wang et al.
(Nature. 2019 May;569(7755):270-274). who demonstrated that ICB-activated CD8⁺
T cells can directly sensitize tumors to ferroptosis via IFN-γ secretion, our in vivo
results indicate that GBP2 knockout reduces both CTL-mediated ferroptosis and anti–
PD-L1 efficacy (Fig. 2A-B).
While our current data cannot fully resolve whether GBP2 acts primarily as a
general enhancer of T cell cytotoxicity or as an ICB-specific regulator, they clearly
establish that GBP2 both augments T cell–mediated killing and amplifies ICB-induced
tumor elimination through CD8⁺ T cell–driven ferroptosis. We acknowledge that the
original manuscript provided suboptimal mechanistic resolution; therefore, we have
substantially revised the text to clarify GBP2’s dual role. Notably, given its ability to
enhance CTL-mediated cytotoxicity, future studies should explore whether GBP2
modulation can be harnessed to improve CAR-T cell efficacy.

We sincerely thank the reviewer for this critical insight. We acknowledge that our study
has not yet definitively established ferroptosis as the primary mechanism through
which GBP2 potentiates ICB efficacy. First, to further identify the specific cytokine
mediating this effect, we generated perforin-/-, IFNγ-/-, or TNFα-/- OT-1 cells and co-

of GBP2-overexpressing tumors (Fig. 2L). Furthermore, we performed blocking

pathways (e.g., pyroptosis, necroptosis, apoptosis) (J Hematol Oncol. 2020 Aug

pyroptosis (disulfiram) showed no such effects (Fig. 2E). These results demonstrate

elimination through ferroptosis.

7. The claim that SHP1 sequestration within GBP2 condensates blocks its function is
not directly supported by the current data. Experiments demonstrating endogenous
co-localization of GBP2 and SHP1 (e.g., via high-resolution imaging) are needed.
Additionally, in vitro assays (such as reconstituted phosphorylation assays) showing
that GBP2 condensates sequester SHP1 and impair STAT1 phosphorylation would
strengthen this claim.
Response:
We thank the reviewer’ s constructive suggestion. Following the reviewer’s
suggestions, we conducted super-resolution imaging and in vitro reconstituted
phosphorylation assays to substantiate the claim that SHP1 sequestration within
GBP2 condensates inhibits its ability to dephosphorylate STAT1. First, high-resolution
imaging (e.g., super-resolution microscopy) demonstrated endogenous co-localization
of GBP2 and SHP1 in cells, confirming that GBP2 condensates physically sequester
SHP1 under physiological conditions (Fig. 5G). These results revealed a clear spatial
association, with SHP1 enriched within GBP2 condensates, supporting our core
hypothesis of sequestration.
Subsequently, we purified recombinant GBP2, SHP1, JAK2, and STAT1 using E. coli,
293T, and Sf9 expression systems to obtain high-purity proteins. Following
established protocols (J Biol Chem. 1995 Sep 1;270(35):20775-80), we established
an in vitro phase separation system by pre-incubating GBP2 to form condensates,
followed by the addition of SHP1 to allow potential sequestration. In parallel, we
performed in vitro kinase reactions by incubating STAT1, JAK2, and ATP at 25°C for
30 minutes. The phase separation system was then combined with the kinase reaction
system in a HEPES reaction buffer (25 mM HEPES, pH 6.5, 50 mM NaCl, 10 mM 2-
mercaptoethanol) for 10 minutes at room temperature to allow STAT1
dephosphorylation. Reactions were terminated by boiling in SDS sample buffer for 5
minutes. STAT1 phosphorylation was analyzed by Western blot using anti-phospho-
STAT1 (Tyr701) antibodies, comparing conditions with and without GBP2
condensates. In the absence of GBP2 condensates, phospho-STAT1 levels were
reduced, indicating active dephosphorylation by SHP1. In contrast, sustained STAT1
phosphorylation was observed in the presence of GBP2 condensates, demonstrating
that SHP1 sequestration within GBP2 condensates impairs its ability to
dephosphorylate STAT1 (Fig. 5H). These findings provide robust evidence supporting
the functional inhibition of SHP1 by GBP2 condensate sequestration.

suggestions for testing the role of phase separation in GBP2 function, we considered
mutating specific amino acids in GBP2 to alter its electrostatic and hydrophobic
properties. However, due to concerns based on prior literature indicating that such
mutations could disrupt protein’s overall structure and
function(https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2021.12.16.472976v1), we opted
not to pursue this approach to avoid confounding effects on protein integrity. Instead,
we fused GBP2 to a hydrophilic MBP sequence to dampen self-association while
preserving the internal sequence. This fusion protein was tested in vitro, revealing
reduced condensate formation and impaired SHP1 sequestration, which led to
sustained STAT1 phosphorylation compared to wild-type GBP2 (Fig. 5J). Moreover,
similar effects were observed in the IDR-deletion group (Fig. 5I). These results
demonstrate that GBP2’s phase separation is critical for its ability to sequester SHP1
and modulate STAT1 signaling, robustly supporting our claims regarding the functional
role of phase separation.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The mechanisms underlying the limited response to immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) remain unclear. One explanation is that tumors escape cytotoxic T cell killing by disrupting interferon-gamma (IFN-γ) signaling. Here we show that guanylate-binding protein 2 (GBP2), an IFN-γ–inducible molecule, functions as a general amplifier of T cell–mediated cytotoxicity by promoting ferroptosis in melanoma. GBP2 enhances STAT1 activation and suppresses SLC7A11, thereby sensitizing tumor cells to ferroptotic death. Upon IFN-γ stimulation, GBP2 undergoes phase separation through an intrinsically disordered region, forming condensates that sequester SHP1 and sustain STAT1 activation. Disrupting GBP2 phase separation impairs ferroptosis, accelerates tumor growth, and weakens T cell–driven tumor control. GBP2 also increases HMGB1 release from ferroptotic cells, promoting cytotoxic T cell infiltration. These findings identify GBP2 as a key mediator linking IFN-γ signaling to ferroptosis and demonstrate that enhancing this pathway can improve tumor responsiveness to ICB immunotherapy.

---

## Introduction

Immune checkpoint blockade (ICB), exemplified by inhibitors targeting programmed cell death 1 (PD-1) or programmed death ligand 1 (PD-L1), has emerged as a transformative therapeutic approach1. ICB therapy restores or enhances the function of effector CD8+T cells (cytotoxic T lymphocytes, CTL) and drives interferon-γ (IFN-γ) production to eliminate tumor cells. Despite substantial clinical success, a significant subset of melanoma patients exhibit suboptimal responses. The pre-existing immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) remains a major barrier to efficacy, driven by factors such as low expression of immune checkpoints and neoantigens, genomic instability, tumor mutational burden, limited infiltration of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs), and attenuated IFN-γ gene signature2,3. These challenges underscore the urgent need for combinatorial strategies capable of overcoming TME‑associated resistance and broadening the benefit of ICB.

One promising approach to elicit this transformation is to induce ferroptosis in tumor cells. Ferroptosis is an iron‑dependent form of cell death driven by lethal accumulation of lipid peroxides4. Multiple strategies have been employed to trigger ferroptosis, including inhibition or degradation of ferroptosis suppressor glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4), development of novel sensitizers for ferroptosis suppressor protein 1 (FSP1), blockade of system X −, and therapeutic cancer nanovaccines—all of which have shown synergistic effects with ICB therapy in preclinical cancer models5. Recently, Wang et al. demonstrated that type II IFN signaling serves as an effective entry point to amplify ferroptosis6. However, the precise molecular mechanisms by which IFN-γ enhances ferroptosis remain poorly understood.

Emerging evidence suggests that many molecular assemblies form membraneless biomolecular condensates via phase separation, offering an insight into previously unexplained biological phenomena7–9. Dysregulated phase separation has been increasingly recognized as a key contributor to cancer progression, including modulation of immune responses8,10,11. Moreover, recent studies indicate that phase separation can facilitate ferroptosis, raising the possibility that this process may serve as a regulatory hub12,13. Nonetheless, the mechanisms by which phase separation selectively compartmentalizes signaling components to control ferroptotic activity remain largely elusive.

In this study, to identify candidate targets for combinatorial immunotherapy, we applied weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA) to screen hub genes associated with IFN-γ response and CTL cytolytic activity. Guanylate binding protein 2 (GBP2) was emerged as a key gene of interest. We observed that GBP2 expression positively correlated with CTL cytotoxicity and infiltration. GBP2 overexpression enhanced, whereas GBP2 deletion attenuated, ferroptosis induced by ICB‑activated CTLs. Mechanistically, we reveal an IFN‑γ–dependent pathway in which tumor cell GBP2 undergoes phase separation, sequestering SHP1 to promote STAT1 phosphorylation. This signaling cascade drives immunogenic ferroptosis, thereby potentiating the efficacy of anti–PD‑L1 immunotherapy. Our findings establish GBP2 phase separation as a previously unrecognized molecular circuit that mediates IFN-γ-dependent ferroptosis and highlight GBP2 as a promising target for combinatorial melanoma immunotherapy.

---

## Results

WGCNA identified GBP2 as a CTL cytolytic activity associated gene in melanoma

ICB therapy primarily eliminates tumor cells by enhancing the effector function of CTL. Activated CTLs engage multiple cytolytic pathways, including IFN-γ, perforin-granzyme, and Fas-Fas ligand signaling to eradicate tumor cells14. However, tumors frequently evade this immune pressure by impairing CTL cytolytic activity—either through inducing T cell dysfunction in CTL-high tumors or by preventing T cell infiltration in CTL-low tumors6. To identify molecular targets associated with CTL cytolytic activity, we employed WGCNA, a robust strategy for screening candidate genes linked to phenotypic traits15. Fifteen co‑expression modules were identified (Figs. 1A and S1). Among them, the yellow module exhibited the strongest correlation with 6-gene-IFN-γ signature (R=0.89, P=4e-29), cytolytic activity signature (R=0.81, P=7e-21) and two independent cytotoxic cell signatures (R=0.86, P=9e-26 and R=0.81, P=3e-20), as determined by module eigengene analysis (Fig. 1B and Supplementary Dataset 1). These signatures collectively predict CTL cytolytic activity16–19. Gene Ontology biological process (GO-BP) analysis further revealed that yellow module genes were significantly enriched in immune regulation, cell killing and IFN-γ response (Fig. 1C). These findings indicate that the yellow module represents a central network associated with CTL cytotoxicity, warranting further interrogation of its constituent genes for hub gene identification.

GO molecular function (MF) analysis showed additional enrichment of GTP binding and GTPase activity in the yellow module (Fig. 1C). GTP-binding proteins regulate a wide range of cellular processes, and elevated GTP levels have recently been linked to be associated with tumor progression, chemotherapy resistance, and ICB resistance20–22. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of the PRJEB23709 cohort demonstrated that GTPase activity and GTP binding were significantly positive enriched in ICB responders (Fig. 1D). Based on this, all yellow module genes were intersected with known GTP-binding proteins, yielding 18 candidates (Fig. 1E). Univariate Cox analysis identified guanylate binding protein 2 (GBP2) as the gene most significantly associated with overall survival (OS) in melanoma patients (Fig. 1F). This finding was validated in GSE8401, GSE59455, and GSE54467 cohorts, with consistent results (Fig. S2A–C). In the GSE65904 cohort, patients with low GBP2 expression exhibited shorter distant metastasis free survival (DMFS) and disease-specific survival (DSS) compared to those with high GBP2 expression (Fig. S2D).

We next examined the relationship between GBP2 expression and clinical features. In the GSE3189 dataset, GBP2 expression was significantly higher in normal tissues than in melanoma tissues (Fig. S2E). Spatial transcriptomic analysis of a melanoma specimen, segmented into malignant, boundary and non-malignant regions and annotated with 10 cell types, revealed that GBP2 was predominantly expressed in normal epithelial cells, with markedly lower levels in malignant regions (Fig. 1G–I). Analysis of major pathological prognostic factors demonstrated that higher GBP2 expression was associated with favorable clinical features, including reduced Breslow thickness, lower Clark level and ulceration—all indicators of better prognosis (Fig. S2F)23,24. To explore the potential biological functions of GBP2 in melanoma, we conducted GSEA and GO analyses. Across six independent cohorts, patients with high GBP2 expression showed significant enrichment in IFN-γ response, regulation of immunity and cell killing (Figs. S3 and S4). Together, these bioinformatic findings in clinical samples identify GBP2 as a potential prognostic biomarker and reveal its close association with CTL cytolytic activity in melanoma.

GBP2 deletion inhibited the CTL-induced ferroptosis to blunt the efficacy of ICB

We next investigated the relationship between GBP2 and ICB responsiveness in melanoma. GBP2 knockout (GBP2−/−) lines were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 in B16-ovalbumin (OVA). GBP2 overexpressing (GBP2oe) lines were established via lentiviral transduction in both B16-ovalbumin (OVA) and A375 cells (Fig. S5A, B and Supplementary Table 1). To investigate the role of GBP2 in antitumor immunity, we first assessed its function in immunodeficient NOD. Cg-Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ (NSG) mice. GBP2 knockout exhibited growth kinetics comparable to control tumors, indicating that GBP2 does not influence tumor progression in the absence of adaptive immunity (Fig. S5C). This finding suggests that GBP2 may exert its antitumor function through modulating adaptive immune responses, particularly CD8⁺ T cell–mediated cytotoxicity. To assess the contribution of GBP2 to T cell–mediated tumor control, OVA‑specific CD8+ (OT‑1) T cells were adoptively transferred into mice bearing either control or GBP2−/− B16‑OVA tumors. OT‑1 transfer effectively suppressed the growth of control tumor growth; however, this effect was markedly diminished in GBP2−/− tumors (Fig. 2A, B). These findings suggest that GBP2 is essential for optimal CD8+ T‑cell–mediated tumor rejection, prompting evaluation of its role in ICB efficacy.

To this end, mice bearing GBP2−/− or sgCtrl B16-OVA tumors were treated with anti-PD-L1 blockade. GBP2 deficiency significantly reduced the antitumor efficacy of anti–PD‑L1 therapy compared to sgCtrl tumors (Fig. 2C, D). Similar results were observed in GBP2‑knockout MC38 tumors, in which GBP2 loss attenuated the response to combined OT‑1 transfer and anti–PD‑L1 treatment (Fig. S5D–H). These data indicate that GBP2 sensitizes tumor cells to CD8+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity, thereby enhancing ICB efficacy in vivo.

Considering that CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) eliminate tumor cells through multiple cell death pathways, we next sought to identify which CTL‑dependent cell death pathways are influenced by GBP2. OT-1 cells were co-cultured with GBP2oe B16-OVA cells in the presence of pathway‑specific inhibitors. Notably, treatment with the ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin‑1 (Fer‑1) significantly attenuated OT‑1-induced cytotoxicity in GBP2oe tumor cells, whereas inhibitors of pan‑caspases (emricasan), necroptosis (necrostatin‑1), or pyroptosis (disulfiram) had no effect (Fig. 2E). Consistently, GSEA revealed a strong positive correlation between GBP2 expression and ferroptosis signatures (Figs. 2F and S6A–E). These findings indicate that GBP2 facilitates CTL-mediated ferroptosis in tumor cells.

To further confirm this association, we measured lipid ROS—a hallmark of ferroptosis—in B16‑OVA tumors. GBP2 knockout tumors from both OT‑1 transfer and anti-PD-L1 treatment groups exhibited reduced lipid ROS levels relative to sgCtrl tumors (Figs. 2G, H and S6F, G). In vitro, GBP2 overexpression enhanced OT-1–induced cytotoxicity and intracellular lipid ROS, effects that were reversed by Fer-1 (Fig. 2I, J). Together, these results demonstrate that GBP2 promotes CTL‑induced ferroptosis and thereby enhances the antitumor efficacy of ICB therapy.

We next investigated the upstream signals through which GBP2 promotes ferroptosis. Given the known role of CD8⁺ T cell secreted cytokines in ICB-induced tumor cell death25, we measured IFN-γ and TNF-α levels in tumors with or without anti–PD‑L1 treatment. Under basal conditions, GBP2 loss had no effect on cytokine levels. At day 7 of anti–PD‑L1 therapy, both IFN-γ and TNF-α showed moderate increases in treated tumors, regardless of GBP2 status (Figs. 2K and S6H). Strikingly, in the late phase of treatment (Day 14), cytokine levels were markedly elevated in control tumors, whereas this increase was blunted in GBP2-deficient tumors, suggesting that GBP2 supports the sustained release of T cell–derived cytokines during late-phase ICB response (Figs. 2K and S6H).

To dissect which cytokine mediates the GBP2-dependent cell death, we co-cultured GBP2-overexpressing tumor cells with OT-1 cells lacking IFN-γ, TNF-α, or perforin. Loss of IFN-γ—but not TNF-α or perforin, abrogated OT‑1-mediated killing of GBP2oe tumor cells (Fig. 2L). These results support previous findings that IFN-γ can trigger ferroptosis in tumor cells and suggest that GBP2 may act within this pathway6,26. Thus, we performed in vivo neutralization experiments. GBP2 overexpression enhanced both anti-PD‑L1 efficacy and lipid ROS accumulation, effects that were completely abolished by anti-IFN‑γ monoclonal antibody treatment, confirming the dependence on IFN-γ signaling (Figs. 2M and S6I). Together, these data suggest that GBP2 acts as a general amplifier of CD8+ T cell–mediated cytotoxicity rather than an ICB-specific effector. GBP2 deficiency attenuated OT-1–driven tumor control even in the absence of PD-L1 blockade, highlighting its fundamental role in IFN-γ–dependent ferroptotic killing of tumor cells. Thus, GBP2 represents a core mediator of T cell cytotoxicity that potentiates the therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade.

GBP2 promotes tumor ferroptosis through STAT1/SLC7A11

We next sought to elucidate the molecular mechanism by which GBP2 regulates IFN-γ-induced ferroptosis. Long-chain-fatty-acid-CoA ligase 4 (ACSL4) is a well-established determinant of ferroptosis27, however, GBP2 depletion did not significantly alter ACSL4 expression (Fig. S7A). The cystine/glutamate antiporter system Xc−, consisting of the light-chain subunit (SLC7A11) and the heavy-chain subunit (SLC3A2), mediates extracellular cystine uptake for antioxidant glutathione (GSH) synthesis, thereby limiting lipid peroxidation and suppressing ferroptosis28,29. To explore whether system Xc− participates in GBP2-mediated ferroptosis regulation in melanoma cells, we examined the expression of its subunits. Compared with sgCtrl cells, sgGBP2 cells displayed a marked attenuation of IFN-γ-induced downregulation of SLC7A11 (Fig. 3A), whereas SLC3A2 expression remained unaffected by GBP2 deletion (Fig. S7B). In situ multi-color immunofluorescence staining of clinical melanoma samples revealed that tumors with high GBP2 expression exhibited lower SLC7A11 levels (Fig. 3B).

To determine whether GBP2 regulates ferroptosis via SLC7A11, we silenced SLC7A11 expression in GBP2−/− cells using siRNA (Fig. S7C and Supplementary Table 2). Upon treatment with the ferroptosis inducer RSL3, SLC7A11 knockdown restored the lipid ROS levels that were reduced by GBP2 deficiency in IFN-γ–primed B16-OVA cells (Fig. 3C). Similarly, GBP2 knockout markedly increased intracellular GSH content and cell viability—effects that were reversed by SLC7A11 silencing (Fig. 3D). In vivo, SLC7A11 overexpression significantly blunted the tumor-suppressive effect of GBP2 overexpression, reduced intratumoral levels of lipid ROS, and abolished its ability to potentiate ICB efficacy (Figs. 3E, F and S7D).

We then investigated the upstream mechanism by which GBP2 represses SLC7A11. Previous studies have implicated the STAT1 signaling pathway in SLC7A11 transcriptional regulation30. We therefore assessed whether GBP2 modulates SLC7A11 expression through STAT1 activation in melanoma. As anticipated, GBP2 depletion markedly reduced phosphorylated STAT1 (p-STAT1) levels in B16-OVA and A375 cells (Fig. 3G). Immunofluorescence imaging and nuclear–cytoplasmic fractionation following IFN-γ stimulation further demonstrated impaired nuclear translocation of p-STAT1 in GBP2−/− cells (Fig. 3H). STAT1 is a central regulator of antitumor immunity, orchestrating key ICB response pathways, including MHC-I antigen presentation, checkpoint ligand expression, and cytotoxic lymphocyte (CD8+ T/NK cell) recognition25. To assess whether STAT1-dependent functions were altered by GBP2 deletion, we examined MHC-I levels in B16-OVA and MC38-OVA cells using the PresentER system, which constitutively co-overexpresses OVA and MHC-I components via peptide/MHC complexes31. As a result, these cells constitutively overexpress both OVA antigen and MHC-I molecules, eliminating the possibility that reduced immunotherapy efficacy in the GBP2-knockout context is due to altered MHC-I presentation. Flow cytometry confirmed comparable MHC-I expression between sgCtrl and sgGBP2 cells (Fig. S7E, F). We next assessed PD-L1 expression. Western blot analysis of sgGBP2 cells revealed no significant difference between sgCtrl and sgGBP2 cells under basal or IFN-γ–stimulated conditions (Fig. S7G). To evaluate potential changes in immune recognition, we employed FucoID technology, which quantifies cell-cell interactions via interaction-dependent fucosyl-biotinylation32. No significant difference in CD8+ T/NK cell–tumor cell interaction frequency was detected between sgCtrl and sgGBP2 groups (Fig. S7H). These findings support that while GBP2 modulates STAT1 activation, it does not affect MHC-I expression, PD-L1 levels, or direct lymphocyte–tumor cell interactions in these models.

Based on these findings, we hypothesize that the STAT1/SLC7A11 axis mediates GBP2-driven ferroptosis. STAT1 has been reported to bind to the SLC7A11 promoter, repressing its transcription6. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) qPCR demonstrated that GBP2 loss abrogated IFN-γ–induced STAT1 binding to the transcription start site of SLC7A11 in B16-OVA and A375 cells (Fig. S7I). More strikingly, STAT1 knockout in GBP2oe B16-OVA cells abolished the increase in lipid ROS, leading to accelerated tumor growth (Figs. 3I–K and S7J). To exclude off-target effects, GBP2 re-expression in GBP2−/− B16-OVA cells significantly rescued SLC7A11 expression and STAT1 phosphorylation (Fig. S7K). Furthermore, enforced GBP2 expression of GBP2 in GBP2-deficient tumor cells restored lipid ROS accumulation and reinstated sensitivity to anti-PD-L1 in vivo (Fig. S7L, M). Together, these results demonstrate that GBP2 promotes ferroptosis by regulating the STAT1/SLC7A11 axis.

GBP2 undergoes phase separation to form condensates

Next, we investigated how GBP2 regulates the STAT1–SLC7A11 axis to promote ferroptosis. Recent studies have implicated phase separation as a critical mechanism triggering ferroptosis, with IFN-γ shown to induce phase separation of key proteins at high concentrations12,13,33,34. Given that GBP2 is an interferon-stimulated gene and that our results demonstrated GBP2 sensitizes tumor cells to IFN-γ-induced ferroptosis, we hypothesized that GBP2 might form biomolecular condensates via phase separation. To test this, we first analyzed the amino acid sequence of the GBP2 protein using the Predictor of Natural Disordered Regions (PONDR)35, which identified residues 436–579 (GBP2436–579) as an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (Fig. 4A). To visualize of GBP2 condensates, we generated B16-OVA and A375 cells with a mCherry tag knocked in at the C terminus of endogenous GBP2. Upon IFN-γ stimulation, endogenous GBP2 formed prominent droplet-like condensates that exhibited fusion and aggregation over time (Figs. 4B, C and S8A, B). We also assessed the dynamic properties of these condensates using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), observing >60% fluorescence recovery within approximately 2 min, indicative of liquid-like mobility (Figs. 4D and S8C). To validate our FRAP methodology, glycogen condensates served as a positive control and mCherry alone as a negative control36,37. Glycogen displayed rapid fluorescence recovery, consistent with known liquid-like dynamics (Fig. S8D), whereas mCherry showed negligible recovery, confirming its non-condensing behavior (Fig. S8E). These controls substantiate the dynamic and fluid nature of GBP2 condensates.

Moreover, treatment with 1,6-hexanediol (1,6-HD), which disrupts liquid–liquid phase separation by interfering with hydrophobic interactions, effectively abolished GBP2 puncta formation (Figs. 4E and S9A). To define the role of the IDR, we generated a deletion mutant lacking residues 436–579 (ΔIDR) in the mCherry-GBP2 construct and expressed it in B16-OVA and A375 cells. Considering the potential destabilization effect of removing this segment, recombinant full-length (FL) and ΔIDR GBP2 proteins were purified from E. coli, with Coomassie staining confirming proper folding of the ΔIDR mutant (Fig. S9B). In GBP2−/− B16-OVA cells transfected with FL or ΔIDR constructs, treatments with proteasomal (MG132), autophagic (BafA1), or lysosomal (chloroquine) inhibitors did not significantly affect GBP2 expression levels (Fig. S9C). Importantly, deletion of GBP2436–579 completely abolished condensate formation (Figs. 4F and S9D). Collectively, these data demonstrate that GBP2 forms the dynamic and reversible phase-separated condensates through its intrinsically disordered region, a property likely integral to its function in regulating ferroptosis.

GBP2 condensates retains SHP1 to protect STAT1 activation to promote ferroptosis

Previous studies have reported that the biomolecular condensates formed via phase separation can spatially restrict protein functions, including nuclear regulation or protein–proteins interactions38. To further elucidate whether GBP2 phase separation facilitates ferroptosis, we performed mass spectrometry to identify GBP2-interacting proteins. As a result, SHP1, a known phosphatase involved in dephosphorylating STAT1 in the IFN-γ signaling pathway39, was detected in GBP2-immunoprecipitates (Fig. 5A). This interaction was validated at both endogenous and exogenous levels by co-immunoprecipitation assays (Figs. 5B and S9E). Functionally, SHP1 knockdown in GBP2−/− cells substantially restored STAT1 phosphorylation and further suppressed SLC7A11 expression (Figs. 5C, S9F and Supplementary Table 2). We hypothesized that GBP2 modulates SHP1 activity through phase separation. Confocal microscopy revealed that GBP2 and SHP1 co-localize within droplet-like condensates in IFN-γ–treated B16-OVA cells, supporting a spatial sequestration model (Fig. 5D).

To investigate the functional relevance of GBP2-SHP1 condensates, we compared full-length GBP2 (FL) with the IDR deletion mutant in GBP2−/− cells. The ΔIDR mutant exhibited diminished IFN-γ–induced phase-separated compartments, accompanied by reduced STAT1 tyrosine phosphorylation and impaired nuclear translocation (Figs. 5E, F and S9G). Correspondingly, IDR deletion led to decreased lipid ROS levels and elevated intracellular GSH upon RSL3 treatment (Fig. S9H, I). Co-immunoprecipitation experiments further demonstrated direct SHP1–STAT1 binding, which was significantly enhanced in GBP2 knockout cells (Fig. S9J). High-resolution imaging confirmed the endogenous co-localization of GBP2 and SHP1 condensates, indicating that GBP2 physically sequesters SHP1 under physiological conditions (Fig. 5G). These findings support our central hypothesis that GBP2 condensates function as spatial regulators by enriching and isolating SHP1. To dissect this mechanism in vitro, we purified recombinant GBP2, SHP1, JAK2, and STAT1 proteins from E. coli, 293T, and Sf9 systems. Pre-formed GBP2 condensates were incubated with SHP1 before assessing STAT1 phosphorylation. Without GBP2 condensates, p-STAT1 levels rapidly decreased due to SHP1-mediated dephosphorylation. In contrast, the presence of GBP2 condensates preserved STAT1 phosphorylation, indicating effective SHP1 sequestration and impaired phosphatase activity (Fig. 5H). Similar results were observed with the ΔIDR mutant, which failed to form condensates and hence could not sequester SHP1 (Fig. 5I). Furthermore, fusion of GBP2 with a hydrophilic maltose-binding protein (MBP) tag to reduce self-association disrupted condensate formation and SHP1 sequestration in vitro, resulting in decreased STAT1 phosphorylation compared to wild-type GBP2 (Fig. 5J). Collectively, these results demonstrate that GBP2 phase separation is essential for sequestering SHP1 and sustaining STAT1 signaling, robustly supporting our claims regarding the functional role of phase separation.

In vivo, introducing GBP2436-579 significantly impaired GBP2-FL-mediated lipid ROS accumulation, accelerated tumor growth, and attenuated anti–PD-L1 therapy efficacy (Fig. 5K, L). Comparable results were observed in OT-1 adoptive cell therapy models (Fig. S10K–M). Co-immunoprecipitation from PD-L1-treated tumors revealed enhanced STAT1-SHP1 binding and decreased STAT1 phosphorylation in GBP2-ΔIDR tumors (Fig. 5M). Furthermore, in vivo phase separation could observe aggregation foci under immunofluorescence36. We performed immunofluorescence staining on these tumor specimens and visualized distinct GBP2 aggregate foci in GBP2-FL tumors following anti-PD-L1 treatment, whereas such structures were absent in GBP2-ΔIDR tumors (Fig. 5N). These findings convincingly demonstrate that CTL-secreted IFN-γ promotes GBP2 phase separation, facilitating SHP1 sequestration, which sustains STAT1 activation, represses SLC7A11 transcription, and induces ferroptosis.

GBP2 promotes the intratumoral CD8+ T cell infiltration through enhancing the immunogenicity of ferroptotic cells

Next, we aimed to investigate the impact of GBP2 on the tumor immune microenvironment (TME) under ICB therapy. We first analyzed the correlation between GBP2 and TME in melanoma patients using the ssGSEA algorithm to estimate the abundance of 28 immune cell types across six cohorts. GBP2 expression was strongly associated with an inflamed immune microenvironment, showing a significant positive correlation primarily with CD8⁺ T cells (Fig. S10A). To validate these findings experimentally, we performed flow cytometry on tumor-infiltrating leukocytes from anti‑PD‑L1–treated sgGBP2 and sgCtrl tumors. Applying the established gating strategies40, we quantified the major immune subsets, including CD8⁺ T cells, CD4⁺ T cells, NK cells, B cells, neutrophils, monocytes/macrophages, and dendritic cells (DCs) (Fig. S10B). Anti-PD-L1 treatment significantly increased the proportions of CD8⁺ T cells, CD4⁺ T cells, NK cells and B cells. Critically, GBP2 deletion substantially reduced infiltration of CD8⁺ T cells regardless of PD-L1 treatment, while CD4⁺ T cells, DCs, B cells, NK cells, macrophages, and neutrophils were unaffected (Fig. 6A). Similarly, flow cytometry revealed that CD8+ OT-1 cell was markedly lower in GBP2-/- tumors compared to controls (Fig. 6B, C). Given the pivotal role of CD8+ T cells in antitumor immunity, we depleted CD8+ T cells in vivo and observed that tumor growth in the oeGBP2 group was increased (Fig. 6D), underscoring the dependence of GBP2-mediated tumor suppression on CD8⁺ T cells. Furthermore, flow cytometric analysis of CD8⁺ T cell activation markers showed that GBP2 ablation markedly attenuated IFN-γ⁺ and TNF-α⁺ CD8⁺ T cell frequencies (Fig. 6E). Analysis of a single-cell RNA sequencing data (GSE115978) from 32 melanoma patients using t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) identified 25 cell clusters into 8 major immune cell types based on canonical marker expression (Fig. S10C). Notably, the five patients with highest GBP2 expression exhibited significantly increased CD8⁺ T cell infiltration (Figs. 6F and S10D). Immunofluorescence staining of further corroborated GBP2-FL tumors following anti-PD-L1 harbored greater CD8⁺ T cell infiltration (Fig. 6G). Collectively, these data demonstrate that GBP2 shapes an immunostimulatory TME, potentiating CD8+ T cell-mediated antitumor immunity.

Recent studies have revealed that ferroptotic tumor cells release damage associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), conferring an immunogenic cell death (ICD)-like phenotype41. Importantly, ICD promotes the recruitment and activation of DCs, which facilitate tumor antigen presentation to CTL, enhancing CD8+ T cell infiltration and activation42. Since GBP2 significantly potentiates CTL-induced ferroptosis, we hypothesized that GBP2 promotes CTL-mediated killing by triggering the ICD feature in ferroptotic tumor cells. To test this, we measured levels of the DAMP high-mobility group box 1 (HMGB1) in tumor tissues from mouse models. ELISA revealed that GBP2 deficiency significantly reduced HMGB1 release under both anti-PD-L1 and OT-1 therapies (Fig. S11A). Concordantly, GBP2−/− tumors exhibited decreased expression of DC maturation markers, including the co-stimulatory molecules CD80 and CD86 (Fig. S11B). Analysis of single-cell data also showed elevated CD86 expression in patients with high GBP2 expression (Fig. S11C). Deletion of STAT1 in GBP2-overexpressing tumors significantly reduced HMGB1 levels, while SLC7A11 overexpression rescued the GBP2-induced HMGB1 upregulation (Fig. S11D, E). Furthermore, HMGB1 knockout in GBP2-overexpressing B16-OVA cells accelerated tumor growth in vivo, accompanied by diminished CD8⁺ OT-1 T cell infiltration and reduced CD80/CD86 expression (Fig. S11F–I). Together, these results suggest that GBP2 enhances the immunogenicity of ferroptotic tumor cells through HMGB1 release, thereby promoting CD8⁺ T cell infiltration in melanoma.

GBP2 facilitates ICB response in tumor patients

Next, we sought to validate the correlation between GBP2 expression and ICB response in human melanoma. We compared three established predictive signatures for ICB response: T cell inflamed expression profile (GEP), innate anti-PD-1 resistance (IPRES) and immuno-predictive score (IMPRES) signatures43–45. Higher enrichment scores of all three signatures were observed in the high GBP2 expression group across multiple melanoma cohorts (Figs. 7A and S12A–D). Using SubMap analysis to compare GBP2 expression profiles with a published melanoma immunotherapy dataset46, the high GBP2 group demonstrated significant similarity to the PD-1 responder group across five cohorts (Figs. 7B and S12E–H). Additionally, we analyzed a cohort comprising pre-treatment (PRE) biopsies taken prior to immunotherapy (n=73), and early during treatment (EDT) samples (7–14 days post-treatment initiation, n=18) (Supplementary Dataset 2). PRE samples with high GBP2 expression exhibited markedly improved clinical responses to ICB compared to low GBP2 samples. Conversely, patients with high SLC7A11 expression showed increased ICB resistance (Figs. 7C and S13A). More importantly, stratifying PRE samples by GBP2 and SLC7A11 expression yielded three groups: group 1 (high GBP2/low SLC7A11), group 2 (low GBP2/low SLC7A11 or high GBP2/high SLC7A11), and group 3 (low GBP2/high SLC7A11). Group 1 displayed the highest percentage of complete or partial responses (CR/PR), while group 3 had the lowest (Fig. 7D). Due to limited EDT samples, direct comparison revealed elevated GBP2 expression in ICB responders versus non-responders (Fig. S13B). Survival analyses indicated that among ICB-treated patients, the high GBP2 group had superior prognosis compared to the low GBP2 group, whereas high SLC7A11 predicted poorer outcomes (Figs. 7E and S13C). Moreover, group 1 exhibited the most favorable survival outcome, followed by group 2, with group 3 demonstrating the shortest OS (Fig. 7F). Similar patterns of elevated GBP2 expression in ICB responders were observed in metastatic urothelial carcinoma and non-small cell lung cancer cohorts47,48, where high GBP2 expression also predicted better prognosis (Fig. S13D, E).

To explore spatial heterogeneity, we analyzed spatial transcriptomics data from a hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) dataset, dividing tissue slices into malignant, boundary, and non-malignant regions (Figs. 7G and S13F). Responders exhibited higher GBP2 and lower SLC7A11 expression in malignant areas, accompanied by increased CD8⁺ T cell infiltration, compared to non-responders (Figs. 7H and S13G). Finally, immunohistochemistry (IHC) of melanoma samples validated that high GBP2 expression correlated with reduced SLC7A11 levels (Fig. 7I). Together, these findings indicate that elevated GBP2 predicts improved OS and better ICB response in tumor patients.
